OIS markets are broadly pricing a larger and faster tightening than our forecasts across most DMs, with expectations of hikes extending into 1H27 and only a modest amount of easing priced for 2H27. This week, the ECB delivered a 25bp hike, taking the depo rate to 2.25%. The hawkish forecast revisions were offset by Lagarde’s data-dependent language which led to limited market reaction, although leaving a sense that more hikes are in the pipeline. At next week’s central bank meetings, we only expect the BoJ to deliver a widely anticipated hike to 1%, while others (Fed, BoE, Riksbank, Norges Bank and RBA) will likely keep rates unchanged. On the Middle East conflict, despite the recent media reports of an MOU agreement, visibility around the likelihood of a ‘deal’ is low and we believe that risks remain skewed more towards the ongoing status quo and Strait of Hormuz limbo. We continue to expect EUR and GBP rates to range trade and our strategy is to favour long positions when valuations are close to levels projected in our energy price spike scenario. What is driving the USD? International conflict remains a key driver of the USD, as reflected in our narrative map. However, the longer the conflict in Iran persists, the more it is likely to feed through into economic data. As a result, the labour market and inflation are exerting an increasingly strong influence on DXY. Given that US data have generally surprised to the upside—and increasingly so—it is logical that data are acting as a tailwind, rather than a headwind, for the USD at this juncture. The risk of going long: contained inflation While there are ample reasons to be long the USD, a key short-term downside risk is softer-than-expected US inflation. records.text: Overseas Investors: JGB Demand Supported by FX Forward Carry May Ease If some overseas investors raise short-term JPY funding using USD via the FX forward market—without matching the maturity of the JGB purchased—they can generate a positive carry of around 2.95% on an annualized basis. Taking advantage of this, these investors can purchase 10-year JGBs at yields of around 2.65%, implying returns of approximately 5.6% and securing around 110bp of excess carry relative to US 10-year Treasuries. Purchasing 30-year JGBs would generate carry of around 6.8%, exceeding US 30-year Treasuries by nearly 180bp. This represents an investment approach that is effectively the reverse of Japanese investors’ hedged foreign bond investment, and appears to have gained traction recently. In this context, as the BoJ proceeds with rate hikes, the carry available through FX forward-based funding is expected to decline, reducing the relative attractiveness of JGBs. As rate hikes progress, purchases of JGBs under such strategies may decline. records.text: M Idea 2 No room for complacency Bottom line | Hold in June: We expect Riksbank to remain on hold on at its June meeting. The Riksbank is in full wait-and-see mode (see Bunge or Hjelm), aided by the good starting point of the economy and fiscal policies. It can afford to wait for more clarity and does not need to act next week, like the ECB did yesterday. Spot inflation surprised to the downside, economic activity in 1Q26 came in weaker than expected and inflation expectations remain anchored. The government also announced multiple fiscal measures in response to the high energy prices, which will lower inflation in the months ahead. Yet, forward looking indicators continue to point towards building inflationary pressures and the uncertainty remains high. The statement will likely reiterate the good starting point of the Riksbank, but underline the increased vigilance and readiness to adjust monetary policy if warranted. Therefore while on a hold, we think the forward guidance will provide more food for thought. Policy rate path: The balance of risks has moved to the upside for the inflation outlook, and we think this will be reflected both in the statement and the revised policy rate path. We expect the new policy rate path to include a possibility of a rate hike already in 3Q26, and price in slightly more than what is now being priced in for 4Q26. records.text: Asia Economic Weekly | 12 June 2026 3 Japan in Focus Takayasu Kudo BofAS Japan Izumi Devalier BofAS Japan See full report: Oil shock: Pipeline pressures set to lift CPI from autumn Pass-through from higher oil prices to CPI to intensify from autumn As a net resource importer, Japan faces additional cost-push pressure from higher import prices. Import prices and PPI rebounded in April-May, and the effect should feed into CPI, which has recently been moderating. Based on autoregression (VAR) analysis, a 10% rise in oil prices lifts gasoline prices from the following month. Electricity follows with a lag of about six months. By contrast, ex- energy BoJ core CPI rises more gradually. The impact peaks about one year after the shock and then persists at a similar pace for roughly another year. In the near term, energy CPI will face upward pressure. But government subsidies should sharply limit the rise. Together with negative food base effects, CPI yoy should continue to moderate through the summer. Even so, cost pressures will continue to spread to non-energy items. Broad-based price increases should lift BoJ core CPI. Our estimates suggest a 1.3–1.4ppt boost to Japan- style core CPI in early 2027, implying a move from below 2% to above 3%. records.text: ge UK Data Comment | Dovish DMP ECB Preview | If in Doubt, Hike Germany Economics & Equity | Trip Notes from Berlin - A Month of Decisions Euro Inflation Watch | Energy Shocks Core: Sneak Preview This week, Jean-Francois Ouvrard discusses ECB communication around EA and Ireland growth data. Next week, the focus will be on the Fed, BoE, Riksbank, and Norges Bank meetings, as well as UK inflation and labor market data. This week in Europe: ECB communication and volatile Ireland GDP figures All eyes this week were on the ECB meeting. As expected, the ECB increased interest rates by 25bp and kept its communication unchanged. The meeting reinforced our conviction that the ECB will pause in July, as only limited new information will be available by then. If oil prices stay elevated, we think the next hike will likely come in September (see our review here). The meeting also delivered updated projections. The ECB revised 2026-27 inflation higher, a touch more than we thought it would. GDP growth was taken a touch lower at 0.8%Y in 2026 (from 0.9%Y in March) and 1.2%Y in 2027 (from 1.3%Y in March). records.text: e, while still having inflation back at target, means they are likely not done yet. That means a short hiking cycle in line with our base case of two hikes, but a third one is possible if there are additional surprises in the data. We still feel comfortable with our call for 50bps in total. Even the adverse scenario could be consistent with a total of 50bp needed to bring inflation back to target by the end of 2028. But the balance of risks has shifted somewhat. A small change in the balance of risks Indeed, the balance of risks is shifting towards a third hike being more likely than “one and done”. For starters, one could argue that even in the mild scenario from the ECB you still need two hikes to bring inflation back to target by the end of 2028. And, while above we argue that the adverse scenario could be seen as consistent with two hikes also, it’s not a clear case and a third could be needed. More importantly, we would push back on the idea of the ECB doing a “one and done” or an “insurance” hike. Lagarde also pushed back against that this week. “One and done” is not unthinkable, but this is a scenario they would arrive at by accident, not something they have in mind today. If they were to skip July and things evolved very positively in the run-up to the September meeting (probably more than in the milder scenario), they could be done at that point. Where do we go next? As a reminder, our expectation, with low conviction, is that they will deliver another hike in July.

The significant decline in FX reserves, adjusted for the forward book and foreign currency liabilities, made BI’s interest rate hikes necessary. This is similar to the situation in 2018, when BI raised interest rates to protect the IDR from excessive depreciation, despite low inflation. We see a risk these hikes start to hurt economic growth at a time when retail sales are already slowing, which would put further negative pressure on the currency. records.text: European Rates Weekly 12 June 2026 Citi Research 7 EMU spreads: Headwinds to tightening We note: (1) the reluctance of EMU spreads to track equities to pre-conflict levels, which we suspect will persist; (2) wider EMU spreads stand out as one of the most consistent seasonal patterns between now and end-August; and (3) at a country level, OATs and BTPs face a relatively high net supply profile over June-August, although the latter is front-loaded. Collectively, these observations reinforce our view that there is limited tightening potential for EMU spreads for now, with technical headwinds especially strong for OATs. Note, this article reiterates and updates content from our daily publications this week (see here and here). (1) EMU spreads becoming reluctant to follow equities higher Limited tightening potential for EMU spreads. While EMU spreads (to Bunds) remain sensitive to broader risk sentiment, our view over the last couple of months has been that these differentials were unlikely to return to pre-conflict levels even if equities did (see here and here). As Figure 9 shows, such a decoupling has played out, indicative of a lower beta of EMU spreads to equities in risk-on and a higher beta in risk-off. records.text: Despite the seemingly positive development on Thursday and the ensuing rally in yields, we see limited scope for a full retracement to pre-war levels given pipeline pricing pressures already in train, the fiscal boost in 2H, and the likelihood that the Riksbank would retain some tightening bias even in a de-escalation scenario. We would look to add outright paid positions when front-end yields move towards pricing cumulative one hike or less or 1Yx1Y Stibor yield moves toward the lower end of a (2.50%, 2.90%) range for 1Yx1Y Stibor. At current levels (2.63%), we stay on the sidelines. Theme 2: Cross-market - pay Sweden versus Euro atr n the front end We continue to favour paying Stibor rates versus Euribor. Riksbank pricing should remain sticky and biased higher. The combination of firming growth, rising pricing surveys, and an explicitly hawkish tilt from the Board means the ~30bp cumulative by Dec26 meeting is unlikely to retrace materially lower, and could drift higher as upcoming inflation prints con- firm pipeline pressures feeding through. We believe, in the medium term, paying Stibor vs Euribor looks attractive if the spread is above 50bp as we find risks tilted towards policy rate convergence (either back to 25bp of policy rate differential or less if inflation is stronger than expected in Sweden) rather than further divergence. records.text: 4 Asia Economic Weekly | 12 June 2026 Some food producers and other firms have already announced price hikes from September in response to higher oil prices, and others are likely to follow. This raises the risk of a fresh round of price increases from autumn. The shift is also evident in the analysis. Re-estimating the VAR using data since 2015, the CPI response to a 10% rise in oil prices is about 1.5 times larger. This suggests that the current roughly 50% oil price shock could lift CPI by around 2ppt. Longer term, inflation expectations are key CPI is likely to reaccelerate following the current oil shock. As a temporary supply shock, the medium-term outlook depends on how inflation expectations among firms and households respond. Our BofA inflation expectations indicator shows that expectations, after falling during COVID, rose sharply following the Ukraine shock and subsequent inflation pickup, and have continued to rise. This could amplify the impact of the current energy shock, as firms pass through costs more actively. Inflation expectations are already near 2%. If inflation rises from here, adaptive dynamics raise the risk of an overshoot above 2% that persists. Some BoJ Board members have expressed concern that expectations may continue to rise rather than stabilize at 2%. records.text: US Economics 12 June 2026 Citi Research 2 Payroll employment has clearly picked up over the last three months, with March, April, and May each adding close to 200k jobs. Some alternative jobs data have also been stronger. But it is not clear to us whether seasonally elevated employment levels reflect sustained stronger demand for workers or simply some temporary shifts in employment patterns in a series that has become much more volatile. If anything, some more leading indicators like NFIB hiring plans or initial jobless claims suggest some upcoming pullback in payroll employment. And one important reason to take stronger payroll employment with a grain of salt is that the unemployment rate has moved sideways at 4.3%, despite three months of job growth running well above what should be a much lower breakeven rate this year. A stable unemployment rate and subdued wage growth at least suggest that recent data do not reflect a retightening in the labor market. We continue to think that a low-hire/low-fire labor market will imply upcoming weaker payroll employment data, with the unemployment rate rising in the summer months. Figure 1. The upstream segments continued to lead, with a surge in prices of raw materials and mining, while overall manufacturing inflation remained more subdued. While the near-term environment is tilting toward Scenario 2, we do not expect a clean “Goldilocks” outcome. Instead, the balance of risks points toward a “soft stagflation-lite” regime, characterised by moderating but fragile growth and elevated inflation. records.text: yield curve is important to discount a bond’s cash flows to get curve-implied yield and par curve is to gauge constant maturity tenor yield. Rich/cheap analysis compares each bond’s market yield with its curve-implied yield to identify bonds trading away from fair value. We calculate seasonally adjusted Breakevens by taking a difference between Treasury par curve and a fitted TIPS curve. TIPS yields need seasonal adjustment because its cash flows are linked to non- seasonally adjusted CPI. Seasonally adjusted fitted TIPS curve help identify rich/cheap bonds using residual 3m z-scores. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear 211/06/2026 ▪ Extended event coverage: All soccer World Cups and Summer/Winter Olympics between 1990 and 2024, totaling 29 events. ▪ Partial-host innovation: The 2026 World Cup is the first to split hosting duties across three countries with materially different match allocations. We introduce a proportional scaling factor to differentiate the inflation impact by match share. The model estimates a panel regression with two-way fixed effects (country and year), identifying the inflation impact of event hosting while controlling for country- specific structural differences and global macroeconomic cycles. The key parameters are the leads (anticipation) and lags (legacy) of the host indicator, which together map the full inflationary arc of a top-tier sports event. World Cup’s inflation arc: Across all soccer World Cups and rounds of Olympic Games in our sample, the model identified a consistent pattern for full host countries. Inflation begins to drift upward approximately three to four years before an event, accelerates through the event year, and peaks one to two years afterward. The maximum cumulative effect in our updated model was approximately 2.1pp, above the BCB’s 1.76pp estimate. This reflects the greater infrastructure intensity of more recent events and the more resilient inflation profile from recent years. Critically, the effect is self-correcting.

records.text: CNY: Trading stronger. Persistent CNY strength has been one of the factors that has n held back broader Dollar appreciation, and we expect CNY strength to extend in the months ahead. Given the highly undervalued levels of the currency and China’s trade competitiveness, policymakers should be, and are proving, more tolerant of gradual currency strength. And so far at least, the ructions in the global economy as a result of the Iran-US war and the modest real appreciation of the currency have proved to be a hiccup rather than a setback to the trade engine. Latest data from May suggested that the trade surplus increased after a drop in April, back above the US$100bn mark, to US$105.6bn in May (seasonally adjusted), vs. US$97.7bn in April. Looking across major destinations also paints a picture of relatively resilient growth despite the energy shock, with nominal exports increasing to most parts of the world with the exception of Europe and Latin America, although most of that increase reflected an increase in prices of tech-related products. Stepping back, while China’s trade surplus may face some near-term headwinds from renewed opportunistic diversification into gold, rising energy/semiconductor import costs, and higher PPI inflation, the structural story across the green technology chain and broader manufacturing competitiveness seems intact as does the deep currency undervaluation (of more than 20% on our GSDEER & GSFEER metrics). However, the metal prices boom has not been accompanied by a proportional increase in investment, as a result of persistent political instability, which keeps increases in volumes constrained. In that sense, the result of the election this week might cause some concern. Even if the right- wing candidate Keiko Fujimori appears to have the edge in the election, marking a shifts towards a business-friendly administration, the tightness of the result (just 1303 votes) risks becoming a legitimacy issue. Whoever ends up winning an election in these conditions will received a weak mandate, which makes governability problems likely to persist, and tackling them might have non-negligible fiscal costs (see Peru: Electoral Déjà vu). Venezuela is benefiting from the double effect of the increase in international oil prices and the recovery of production due to the easing of sanctions after the US removal of Maduro from office in January. This could result in an increase in oil exports revenues of approximately 50% in 2026. However, it is important to manage expectations. While the country is likely to stay on an improving trend over the coming years, part of the recent increase in oil exports is mainly an statistical rebound from the lows reached last year in the middle of the escalation of tensions with the US. records.text: US Outlook Back on the pitch, updated playbook Beneath a soft core CPI print, underlying inflation is firmer than it appears, with risks skewed upward. Key signals from next week's FOMC meeting are about the reaction function and the new chair's intentions for reshaping policy. Even with Warsh's fresh legs, patience is still the gameplan. • Core CPI printed at 0.21% m/m in May, with weakness in core goods and idiosyncratic• declines in auto insurance exaggerating disinflationary progress. Core PCE looks to run at a much firmer 0.36% m/m, with May's upswing in portfolio management fees exaggerating underlying pressures. In our view, estimates do not yet point to a sustained return to disinflation. • Even amid the recent sharp pickup in measured job gains, activity data generally point to• moderation in demand, with our GDP growth tracker at about 2.5% q/q saar in the current quarter. Next week, we expect both the headline and control group retail sales readings to slow to around 0.2% m/m, with two-sided risks. Industrial production should also slow from April. • We expect the FOMC to remain on hold next week, with the median projection showing higher• inflation in 2026 and a single rate cut in 2027. A solid majority of participants is likely to signal no change this year, with a few still pointing to hikes, and the 2027 outcome a close call. We expect Warsh to leave early imprints, with guidance removed and announcements of reviews of the balance sheet and FOMC communications.

records.text: Global Economic Viewpoint | 11 June 2026 13 Ghana: gold boosted recovery, reform focused future Since 2023, Ghana has moved from crisis to stabilisation following its IMF-backed restructuring, with macro conditions now significantly improved. The authorities have met all IMF Extended Credit Facility (ECF) targets, with the programme entering its final stage ahead of Board approval (expected mid-July). The next phase focuses on locking in gains through a new IMF Policy Coordination Instrument (PCI) to anchor reforms and strengthen policy credibility. External buffers have strengthened materially, with FX reserves rising to around US$14bn (6 months of import cover), supported by a strong balance of payments, particularly elevated gold prices, and initiatives such as the gold purchase programme. There is also a clear push to further diversify FX sources (including cocoa and from oil). The medium-term goal is to build reserves to 15 months of import cover over three years. Despite this, risks remain from energy costs and weaker cocoa performance, while recent cedi volatility reflects short-term FX demand-supply mismatches rather than fundamentals; authorities emphasise a market-determined exchange rate with two-way flexibility while market concerns are on active FX interventions. On inflation and monetary policy, inflation has edged up modestly to 3.7%, with expectations of further increases due to base effects and energy pressures, likely moving toward the medium- term of 6%. We break down how current market conditions compare to the Bank's three scenarios below and what the implications could mean for GDP and CPI. Oil: While oil prices have budged a little relative to the last month, futures pricing remains well behaved for the most part. In fact, Brent futures over the next three years are tracking "only" around 3% higher, relative to the Bank's Scenario A. How do market prices fare relative to the Bank's more hawkish scenarios? Brent futures sit just around 6% below the Bank's assumed Scenario B implied oil price, and nearly 26% below the Bank's Scenario C assumption. How much would this add to GDP and CPI? For GDP, we estimate that changes in oil futures would have a broadly negligible impact on growth. For CPI, we estimate the net impact would be a 1bp increase in 1y-ahead CPI, rising to 3bps in the 2y- ahead forecast. Gas: Similar to oil, gas prices have also been better behaved, relative to either of the Bank's more hawkish scenarios. In fact, gas prices are tracking around, or slightly below, the Bank's Scenario A path. records.text: largest monthly fall on record Source : Deutsche Bank,Macrobond Figure 9: Private sector wage growth already at 3% in Q1-26 Source : Deutsche Bank,Macrobond The price outlook – starting on a softer footing Despite stronger growth to start the year, the weaker UK labour market coincides with a weaker price outlook – something that we think could give many on the MPC confidence to stay on the sidelines for now. What's happened since the April MPR? While the MPC will have seen the May inflation report ahead of its decision, the all-important April report came in a lot better than expected. Indeed, for the first time in six years both headline CPI and core CPI missed consensus expectations. In fact, relative to the Bank of England's forecasts, April CPI came in 0.2pp below expectations on headline (2.8% y-o-y), while services CPI missed by a similar amount, relative to the Bank's projections (3.2% vs 3.4%). We expect May CPI to remain below the Bank's forecasts too, with headline, core, services, and food inflation all nesting meaningfully below the Bank's projections. Survey data, however, paint a more uncomfortable picture. Output prices are rising (though at a slower pace than reported a couple of months ago). Supply chain pressures are also building – which could accentuate price pass-through. This is something the Bank will need to watch closely in assessing the risks of both indirect and/or second-round effects. Provided for the exclusive use of cayla.buettner@bluecrestcapi

records.text: UK: Rates Strategy Every vote counts Two significant votes take place on 18 June — in Makerfield and on Threadneedle Street. The MPC is likely to leave the door open to tightening, but if May's inflation data suggest rising pressures, a more hawkish twist cannot be ruled out. Macro curve steepening remains the path of least resistance. On 18 June monetary policy will coincide with politics, as the Makerfield by-election and the June MPC decision will both take place. Both votes will have wider consequences beyond the immediate decisions, and may well turn out to be market-defining for different reasons — triggering further market discussion over Andy Burnham's potential policies should he win (as the polls currently indicate) and for the MPC as it assess the outlook for the economy before it reconvenes for its July forecast round and rate decision. Our economists expect the policy rate to be left at 3.75% with a 7-2 vote split, with BOE Chief Economist Huw Pill and external member Megan Greene dissenting in favor of a 25bp hike. The concessional FX swaps offered by India will incur a cost for the RBI. This will lead to a decrease in the RBI's annual profits, which in turn should result in a reduction in its dividend payments to the government over time. In essence, the government will indirectly bear the cost of these concessions, which will contribute to a higher fiscal deficit. Q6. How is Bank Indonesia addressing weakness in the rupiah? In a surprise move, BI announced an off-cycle interest rate hike of 25bp on 9 June, following a 50bp increase at its May meeting. This brings the BI rate to 5.5%. In addition to intensifying its traditional FX intervention measures, BI has introduced incentives to reduce swap hedging costs for foreign investors by 10%. This effectively provides a rebate on the current 10% tax paid by foreign investors when investing in Indonesian assets and is aimed at attracting more foreign inflows. We think these measures demonstrate the authorities' growing sense of urgency to stabilize the rupiah. records.text: M Idea 8 Financial Conditions: A near-reversal following the April 7 ceasefire Following the conflict in the Middle East and the uncertainty it brings to the next steps for monetary policy, we include the evolution of our FRB/US-based model of financial conditions, which aims to capture how changes in asset prices weigh on future economic activity. The index includes five daily variables: the 10-year Treasury yield, S&P 500 returns, the corporate BBB credit spread, the valuation of the U.S. dollar, and the price of oil. These are aggregated based on their estimated growth elasticities relative to the federal funds rate, using the Federal Reserve’s FRB/US model. As a result, the index can be interpreted as the equivalent change in the federal funds rate, expressed in basis points, required to generate a similar effect on economic activity. Since hostilities in the Middle East began on February 28, the tightening in financial conditions is equivalent to about a 28bp rise in the federal funds rate. Since the April 7 ceasefire announcement, however, financial conditions have eased by 44bps. The tightening reversed all of the easing seen earlier this year, most of which occurred between the December and January FOMC meetings and was primarily driven by a weaker U.S. dollar. The net tightening since February 28 has been driven mainly by higher 10-year U.S. Treasury yields, with dollar appreciation and higher oil prices playing a secondary role. records.text: US Economics Weekly12 June 2026 ab 12 Peak fiscal support for households Real consumer spending has slowed recently, growing by only 1.6% at an annual rate in the first quarter. This number could be revised even lower when the BEA releases its third estimate of GDP later this month. We expect consumer spending will improve in the second quarter, despite higher gas prices, because fiscal stimulus is likely at its peak. We predicted that the One Big Beautiful Bill Act would boost growth this year, especially through larger tax refunds for people who didn’t update their tax withholding after new rules began last July. To monitor this, we have shown charts in recent months tracking how tax refunds are sent from the US Treasury to households. We expected the extra refunds to total around $60 billion, and the data shows that’s about what happened. These refunds usually start coming in mid-March, ramp up after the April 15 filing deadline, and then slow down by late April or early May. We were concerned that the more complex tax code after the OBBBA and fewer IRS staff through 2025 might delay tax filings and refunds. However, this didn’t turn out to be a major issue, and the timing of refund payments to households has stayed mostly the same this year. According to the latest US Treasury data as of June 10, refunds issued are about $53 billion higher than this time last year, while refunds paid are about $65 billion higher. This revamp is meant to reflect a structural shift in LIC debt profiles, which were predominantly external a decade ago but are now increasingly domestic. As a result, countries where domestic debt has risen sharply could face stronger risk signals under the revised framework. This is particularly relevant for several frontier markets where domestic financing has expanded rapidly, including Senegal, parts of Economic and Monetary Community of Central Africa (CEMAC), and Kenya. The implication is a more comprehensive, but potentially less forgiving, assessment of debt sustainability as domestic vulnerabilities are more systematically captured. Under the previous LIC DSA framework, the analytical focus was predominantly on external debt, while the public DSA often functioned more as a reference benchmark rather than a binding threshold. In practice, however, this distinction was not always clear-cut. In cases such as Ghana, the public DSA was effectively used de facto as a binding constraint, even though the methodology in earlier guidance notes did not explicitly formalise it as such. After approval of the new framework, a transition period of about 9-12 months will be required before full implementation. The market is crying wolf. While uncertainty is high, we would point out that the market’s track record in predicting hikes 6m out is not overly compelling. Figure 17 shows all the events since early 1996 where the market priced 20bp of hikes 6 months out (for at least 3 consecutive days). It also shows the cumulative Fed hikes in the subsequent 6m. We reset the clock if we move back to pricing only 5bp or less. Of the 14 events we find, we find 5 hikes, 3 cuts, and 6 pauses, so the hit ratio is just 35%. It gets even worse if we only focus on the first hike of a cycle (determined as the first hike in a 6m window), which we do as forecasting a hike in an ongoing hiking cycle is presumably a lot easier. Here, we find 4 hits out of a total of 14, i.e. 28% chance to price the first hike correctly. The 5th hike happened in mid-2023 when the market was overeager and priced the end of the hiking cycle, only for the Fed to hike again in July. So, just because the market is crying wolf does not necessarily mean it happens. T o put the question the other way around (when does the market start pricing of the first hike correctly?), we show in Figure 18 that the market is pricing in a first hike around 3-4 months before it happens, in the median case. records.text: 11 June 2026 Asia Local Markets Weekly Deutsche Bank AG/Singapore Page 13 Korea External headwinds remain a hurdle for KTBs Elevated oil prices continue to be a drain to regional governments’ fiscal coffers, including Korea. Given the US-Iran conflict continues, this raises questions about whether Korea’s fuel subsidy program can absorb the shock without requiring additional issuance. Our answer is yes — the fiscal arithmetic holds even under stress. Why? n Refiners have accepted the government’s actual-cost-based compensation method, which has reduced the per-litre subsidy burden. As a result, cumulative subsidy payouts amounted to only ~KRW 1.7tn as of May, against a total allocated budget of KRW 4.2tn. This leaves a significant KRW 2.5tn buffer. Furthermore, the settlement process operates on a 2–3 month lag. This means any extension of the program beyond its current September end-date would likely defer incremental payments into the 2027 budget, avoiding the need for an immediate in-year adjustment. n Under our base case of oil below USD110/bbl, the remaining buffer is sufficient to sustain the subsidy for a further six months in line with our initial assessment in May. Even a stress scenario of oil prices averaging USD 130/bbl for six months appears manageable. While this would create an estimated KRW 5.8tn funding gap, the net shortfall after applying the remaining KRW 2.5tn buffer is only KRW 3.3tn. records.text: Dwyfor Evans 11 June 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Emerging Markets Weekly: Policy Divergence Overtakes Beta Against a backdrop of weak cross -asset flows, EM FX has softened modestly amid USD strength, geopolitics, and increasingly idiosyncratic domestic drivers . This marks a shift from broad beta to policy -driven divergence. Asian central banks have responde d actively: Indonesia combined direct intervention with a surprise rate hike, India expanded FX forwards, and Korea intensified signaling to support the KRW. This indicates rising intervention risk and the need to focus on country-specific policy reactions. Exposure in the FX portfolio has been reduced this week, with shorts in USDTRY, EURILS, and JPYKRW closed as macro stress, policy constraints, and intervention risks increased. Relative value remains preferred. Long CNYINR captures external balance divergence, with CNY supported by structural inflows while INR faces persistent outflows and oil sensitivity. Carry remains selective, favoring BRL and COP on real yields and commodity support. Structural themes also persist, with ASEAN vulnerability contrasting against tech-driven strength in Taiwan. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 3 study of a wide range of Enterprise AI use cases, the average single use would save an Enterprise customer $55 in costs. While it is not possible to precisely know how many tokens will be used to achieve this outcome (and token usage will likely vary significantly across Enterprise use cases), we can ground ourselves in some helpful math. One analysis suggests that a single AI Agent may consume ~15x the tokens relative to a query-based usage of a LLM. A typical query based usage of a LLM would consume ~5,000 tokens. If an Enterprise customer used 5-7 AI Agents to execute an economic task, the token usage would be 375,000-525,000 tokens. Token pricing can be found here — you will see that pricing can range widely among models and between input and output tokens. At an assumed average token price of $3-10 (in general, input tokens will outweigh output tokens, but not always), the cost to execute the economic task would be $2-5, a fraction of the $55 benefit. From the perspective of the LLM developer, based on token pricing that is publicly available, our Blackwell data center would generate margins of ~60%, factoring in all data center costs (but not the cost to develop the LLM). Interestingly, when we run the same math for Rubin and Feynman data centers, the margins would rise to ~80% and 90%, respectively. records.text: Japan Outlook Policy rates headed back to 1% for first time since 1995 We expect the BoJ to raise rates next week, emphasizing upside inflation risks over downside economic risks, then to 1.5% by next spring. In the interim assessment of QT , a halt to the reduction in JGB purchases is expected from FY27 onward. BoJ likely to resume hiking at June MPM, taking the policy rate to 1% At the monetary policy meeting (MPM) to be held on 15-16 June, we expect the BoJ to raise the policy rate from the current 0.75% to 1%, the highest level since 1995. As of the January MPM, we had sensed that concerns within the BoJ Policy Board about JPY depreciation stemming from the exceptionally low real policy rate had risen markedly, and we had therefore expected a rate hike at the April meeting. However, at the time of that meeting, uncertainty surrounding the Middle East situation was extremely high, leaving the BoJ little choice but to wait and see. Into June, however, the process toward agreement has continued, albeit with twists and turns along the way, and the absence of major downward pressure on production and consumption has also been confirmed. We therefore think the BoJ will conclude that it should go ahead with a rate hike without waiting for the July Outlook Report, placing greater weight on its commitment to addressing upside inflation risks. records.text: Derivatives Strategy Preparing for a new Fed chair Do new Fed Chairs deliver bigger surprises on their first meetings than the typical FOMC meeting? The answer is surprisingly nuanced in the context of the upcoming meeting. We also discuss dealer balance sheet expansion in relation to swap spreads. Options: Do new Fed chairs surprise the rates market more than the typical FOMC meeting? The market will face Fed Chair Warsh's first FOMC meeting next week, and one topic of discussion for the vol market has been whether FOMC meetings conducted by new Fed Chairs deliver uniquely large rate market moves. We look at the data for FOMC meetings going back to the Greenspan era and find the answer to be quite nuanced. An important caveat here is that we only have examples of four FOMC meetings chaired by a new Fed chair since 1987, so what follows are general patterns that may not be statistically significant. Have rates moved more on the first FOMC meeting of a new Fed chair than they do on the average FOMC meeting day? The answer is not clear. This can be seen in Figure 1, which looks at absolute moves in 2y and 10y Treasury yields on new Fed Chair FOMC dates and compares them to the average absolute move across all FOMC dates since 1997. In fact, it appears that the 2y yield move on new Fed Chair FOMCs has been smaller than that on typical FOMC dates, but the 10y yield move on such FOMC dates has been somewhat larger. records.text: the Basic Policy could potentially increase issuance from FY2027, making the coming months critical for assessing the administration’s fiscal stance. • JGB Supply: Assuming the current pace of issuance and continued BoJ purchase reduc- tions, market holdings are projected to increase by around JPY 65tn over the next year, concentrated in the 6–10y sector on an outstanding basis. Even if the reduction in BoJ purchases is paused from April 2027 onward, BoJ holdings are still expected to decline materially, implying QT will continue at a pace exceeding JPY 40tn per year. • JPY Rates Market Outlook: The up to 5y sector is likely to remain stable with steady demand, while the 6–10y sector faces the strongest supply pressure and is expected to underperform, with 10-year yields trending toward 3%. Although the super-long sector has seen improved supply-demand conditions, structural demand remains weak due to reliance on overseas and pension flows and exposure to fiscal risks. • Investor Behavior: While rate-hike discussions often focus on yield-curve implica- tions, rising rates themselves can weigh on JPY bond demand. Banks remain biased toward shorter durations, life insurers face structural constraints on super-long demand, and FX forward carry-supported demand from some overseas investors may ease as rate hikes erode that advantage, suggesting that overall duration demand is likely to remain constrained. • Swap Spreads: Front-end swap spreads are likely to remain range-bound. records.text: ased on current polls Milestone #3 – landslide victory of the far-right AfD in September local elections largely priced in. The AfD is currently polling at 42% in Saxony-Anhalt and 36% in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. This seems far from an absolute majority. But if several of the smaller parties miss the 5% threshold, an election outcome of around 40% could be sufficient to achieve such a majority. Thus, the AfD might govern an Eastern state with an absolute majority for the first time ever. But even a landslide victory of the far-right is very unlikely to be a catalyst for tensions in the Merz government. Both Eastern states are relatively small (accounting for 5% of the electorate) and the federal coalition would likely try to frame this as regional specifics. Reform momentum (e.g. regarding pension reform) might stall for a couple of weeks until this new political reality is digested. The third milestone is the most important to watch in terms of coalition stability. While a landslide victory by the far-right AfD is largely priced in by all political actors, changes to key personnel cannot be ruled in the aftermath of a potentially devastating electoral loss for the two ruling parties. Governor Ueda’s recent speech—combined with the dissents, projections, and statement of the April meeting—essentially previewed the hike, so the bar for a hawkish surprise is high. Though with Ueda not able to deliver the press conference (Deputy Governor Uchida will be filling in), it may be harder to decipher whether any marginal communication shift is intentional or not. But in any case, without a guide towards a faster pace of hikes, markets will remain most focused on the JPY-negative fundamentals of constrained monetary policy, higher-for-longer US yields, US growth outperformance, and domestic fiscal risks. Current balance sheet policy is also set to be reassessed at this meeting, and some have speculated that the Board may consider an increase to JGB purchases to contain long-end yields. But we think that would only add to the downward pressure on the currency (which the MoF wants to avoid), especially since rising fiscal risk premium has been the driver of higher yields rather than supply. For that reason and the fact that bond market functioning has been improving, our economists think the BoJ will stick to its previously decided plan to reduce purchases to a pace of ¥200bn per quarter. records.text: Ueda’s communication on 3 June, the final scheduled speech by a Policy Board member before the June meeting. In his 3 June speech, Governor Ueda avoided a “pre-commitment” but showed strong willingness to raise rates Ahead of the December 2025 meeting, at which the BoJ decided to raise rates, Governor Ueda said in a speech that he wanted to “appropriately assess” the pros and cons of a rate hike, leading the market to price one to a substantial degree. This time, he cited a need to “thoroughly discuss” whether to raise rates. By replacing “judge” with “discuss, ” he appears to have been in less of a “pre-commitment” mode this time, and in that sense may have left the option of no change on the table. At the same time, however, by changing “appropriately (judge)” to “thoroughly (discuss), ” we view this as suggesting a relatively strong willingness to move toward a rate hike. A strong warning on upside inflation risks, including behind-the-curve risk Throughout the speech, he also appeared to be highly alert to upside inflation risks. First, he said that the price pass-through stemming from higher oil prices is likely to spread more quickly and broadly than before, and that compared with other major economies and with Japan in the past, conditions are such that “second-round effects” are more likely to lead to upside pressure on underlying inflation. records.text: econcile the above with the market pricing in hikes? We believe that boils down to the difference in inflation forecasts. Figure 5 shows what the CPI swaps market are pricing in for 1y ex-energy CPI inflation at different forward dates. 1y1y CPI swaps are implying core inflation of 2.7%. Usually, PCE runs below CPI, but given the change in composition (drag from housing and boost from goods inflation), PCE and CPI are expected to remain on top of each other even into next year. Hence, the markets are likely expecting inflation to exceed the Fed's median forecasts by 40bp or so in 2027. In a typical Taylor rule, that justifies a 50-60bp higher rate. Hence, while the market will likely look "cheap" to the June dots, that largely would be a reflection of a different inflation forecast. One should therefore not interpret the 2027 dot showing a 25bp cut next year as a dovish outcome versus market pricing. It would be dovish if the Fed forecast 50bp in cuts next year even as it revises higher its inflation forecast, and on the other hand, it would be hawkish if the Fed forecast no cuts through the entire forecast horizon even as it expected inflation to get near 2% by end of 2027. Taking advantage of this, these investors can purchase 10-year JGBs at yields of around 2.65%, implying returns of approximately 5.6% and securing around 110bp of excess carry relative to US 10-year Treasuries. Purchas- ing 30-year JGBs would generate carry of around 6.8%, exceeding US 30-year Treasuries by nearly 180bp. This represents an investment approach that is effectively the reverse of Japanese investors’ hedged foreign bond investment, and appears to have gained traction recently. In this con- text, as the BoJ proceeds with rate hikes, the carry available through FX forward-based funding is expected to decline, reducing the relative attractiveness of JGBs. records.text: Saipem SPA (SPMI.MI) – Buy Target Price: €5.10, ETR +19% Investment Thesis & Key Themes – We rate Saipem Buy/High Risk ahead of the proposed merger with Subsea7 (expected 2H26). In our view, the combined entity will be well positioned to unlock incremental synergies, building on businesses that are already demonstrating improved commercial discipline across key end-markets. Saipem currently trades at a discount to its European oilfield services peers, despite clear evidence of margin recovery and increasing exposure to offshore activity. We continue to see upside across the European offshore services complex, supported by resilient project backlogs and ongoing margin improvement, which we believe signals a mid-upcycle positioning. Key Debates / Pushback – Key areas of investor debate are likely to focus on whether the pro forma entity’s valuation discount to US peers is justified given execution and integration risks; the degree of Middle East exposure and associated concentration risk; and the persistence of an “Italian discount” in the equity story. There is also ongoing scrutiny around Saipem’s historical execution, particularly legacy project overruns, alongside risks to deal completion (including competition approvals) and subsequent integration delivery. Finally, some investors may question the investment case given Saipem’s diversified business mix, which limits its positioning as a pure-play offshore services name. Valuation – Saipem trades on a valuation of 3.4x 2028

records.text: China Outlook Mixed data, weak pass-through May data painted a mixed picture, with strong exports offsetting weak consumption and housing. Despite higher oil- driven PPI, pass-through to CPI remains limited, reflecting firms' difficulty in passing on costs. Retail sales and FAI are set to weaken further, while IP is set to rebound on exports. Following the broad-based slowdown in April, major economic indicators released this week and high-frequency data for May painted a mixed picture, though on balance still pointing to a slowdown in growth momentum in Q2. Export growth accelerated and significantly exceeded market expectations, while softer-than-expected CPI inflation, slower credit growth and a deeper contraction in auto sales pointed to weak consumption, and the weak new property sales confirmed that the rebound in the housing market is short-lived. Next week, we expect retail sales and fixed asset investment to weaken further as the impact of front-loaded fiscal stimulus fades. Moreover, despite the Middle East conflict lasting more than three months, May PPI and CPI data continued to suggest limited pass-through from higher oil and petrochemical-related raw material prices—which pushed up PPI significantly to 3.9% y/y—to consumer goods and services, with core CPI edging down to 1.1% y/y in May, remaining below its pre-conflict average of 1.3% in January–February. These highlight a more active policy response to the twin pressures of higher oil prices and a rates -driven USD cycle. records.text: Euro Area: Rates Strategy Don't call it an insurance hike The ECB delivered its first 25bp hike since September 23, with inflation and growth revisions hawkish at the margin. That said, it offered little guidance on if and when it will follow with more, though risks seemed skewed towards further action, barring a quick improvement in the inflation outlook. Exhaustion. Another week is drawing to a close without a resolution to the Middle East conflict, this time with the ceasefire failing to hold, as strikes have resumed. Yet the market appears increasingly less sensitive to the continued headline tennis. It seems to have found some comfort in the idea that, despite the tit-for-tat, risks of a more serious escalation remain contained, with Trump's repeated references to an imminent deal still seen as somewhat credible. So even in the face of renewed tensions, and before the shift towards more positive headlines, it is striking that oil was little changed so far this week, and so too were front-end rates. That said, markets continue to price high(-er) for longer oil prices, with flatter (ie, less backwardated) curves offering little support for a rapid disinflation in energy. In that sense, the current setup is no panacea for inflation and is likely to keep central banks on their toes. records.text: 14 Global Economic Weekly | 12 June 2026 Firms are pricing more aggressively Pass-through from import prices to CPI has strengthened in recent years, likely due to both rising import penetration and more active pricing by firms than in the past. Some food producers and other firms have already announced price hikes from September in response to higher oil prices, and others are likely to follow. This raises the risk of a fresh round of price increases from autumn. The shift is also evident in the analysis. Re-estimating the VAR using data since 2015, the CPI response to a 10% rise in oil prices is about 1.5 times larger. This suggests that the current roughly 50% oil price shock could lift CPI by around 2ppt. Longer term, inflation expectations are key CPI is likely to reaccelerate following the current oil shock. As a temporary supply shock, the medium-term outlook depends on how inflation expectations among firms and households respond. Our BofA inflation expectations indicator shows that expectations, after falling during COVID, rose sharply following the Ukraine shock and subsequent inflation pickup, and have continued to rise. This could amplify the impact of the current energy shock, as firms pass through costs more actively. Inflation expectations are already near 2%. If inflation rises from here, adaptive dynamics raise the risk of an overshoot above 2% that persists. Recall that Warsh has criticized forward guidance, data dependence, and the Fed’s models, leaving a narrative -based approach as potentially most relevant. Within this, he could emphasize the importance of productivity growth and AI for providing a strong backdrop for supply-side growth that – over time – could prove to be disinflationary. Warsh is also likely to highlight some aspects of the inflation outlook that are less concerning, including softer measures of trend inflation, moderating wage growth, stable labor market slack, shelter disinflation, and the potential for tariff price pressures to abate over time. That said, we do not anticipate an overtly dovish message from Warsh – e.g., we do not expect him to lean excessively on measures like trimmed mean inflation – as doing so would risk a more significant rise in inflation expectations and bond yields in the belly and longer end of the curve. Notably absent from his nomination hearing was a focus on the labor market. While in previous years that side of the dual mandate ha s provided scope for the Fed to lower rates even in the face of elevated inflation, recent data have provided Fed officials with greater confidence that the labor market is at worst stabilizing. One view was that things are different from 2022 with a weak labour market and restrictive rates limiting wage pressures and second round effects, allowing the BoE to look through the shock and keep rates on hold. Another view was that the more persistent the shock is, the more pressure there will be on the BoE to hike, though they would do so reluctantly. Those who believed that the BoE could hike noted that, in the near term, no action is likely. However, they noted that pressure on the BoE to hike could rise in September once inflation rises in July, assuming the energy price rise in persistent (and scenarios could be tweaked to reflect a more persistent shock). Action from other central banks could also influence the reaction function of the BoE. But there was broad based agreement that the BoE is unlikely to cut this year, even if the conflict resolves. Fiscal challenges are likely to be high Speakers agreed that fiscal challenges are likely to be high, no matter who is in charge. There is limited headroom within the current fiscal rules, with the conflict implying a £10-15bn hit already to the headroom. At the same time, pressures to provide energy support to lower income households will likely rise, along with pressures on defence spending, unprotected departments and volatility in gilt yields. While the event may provide a short-term economic boost localized to the 11 US host cities, we expect relatively little impact on headline GDP , inflation, or labor market figures. In fact, the BLS has confirmed with us that tickets for irregular events like the world cup are not even in scope for the CPI. Available hotel booking data looks mixed. Sojern's world cup 2026 Travel Index cited by a CNBC article shows June 2026 hotel bookings running ahead of last year in all US host cities except Seattle, but the range in estimates is wide. The Sojern data indicates bookings 12% ahead of last June in Houston, but -21% behind last June in Seattle. Other US host cities' bookings are running ahead of last year at a single-digit pace. In other data, the American Hotel & Lodging Association last month found that only 2 of 11 US world cup cities surveyed were seeing bookings above normal, with the majority of travellers being US domestic residents and FIFA continuing to release reservations on rooms previously booked. Broadly, while the 2026 world cup may deliver localized and short-term boosts, especially in already-developed urban centers, the broader national economic impact is likely to be limited, consistent with the experience of past tournaments. We start with all actively traded USTs for a specific date and remove large outliers. Curve construction is more straightforward for swaps than for bonds. Swap instruments are usually available at standard tenors, and there is typically one instrument per tenor. Because of this structure, we can apply bootstrapping from the short end to solve for the zero curve step by step. For Treasuries, the problem is different. There can be multiple bonds in the same maturity area with different coupons, issue dates, liquidity profiles, and yields to maturity. Because of this, we cannot simply bootstrap via one point from each maturity. It's possible, in our minds, that Catherine Mann could join the hawkish contingent on the MPC, advocating for a rate hike. We don't think this would surprise markets. Indeed, if there were to be a hawkish surprise on the vote tally, we would need to see a vote for rate hike from one of the Deputy Governors – Clare Lombardelli and/or Dave Ramsden. The message. Given lingering uncertainty, we expect the MPC's message to be three-fold: One, despite still heightened uncertainty on the path ahead, markets remain more sanguine about energy prices – particularly when compared to the Bank's hawkish scenarios introduced in April. Put simply, this should give the MPC more time to let the dust settle on the energy shock. Two, monetary policy remains in a good place to deal with any changes in the outlook. Rising Bank Rate expectations will continue to weigh on activity and inflation – doing some of the heavy lifting for the BoE. And with large uncertainties lingering around indirect and second-round effects, the need to adjust Bank Rate ahead of summer remains unclear – especially with a still-weakening labour market. records.text: Resilient 2027 Prices vs. Large Surplus We forecast 2027 Brent prices to average $80, or $10 above their 2025 average, despite a record 3.5mb/d 2027 surplus for two reasons. First, OECD commercial oil stocks—a key driver of spot prices vs. long dated prices—are unlikely to reach very high levels in 2027 given a low starting point and a low share of OECD commercial stocks in 2027 global inventory increases. In our base case, OECD commercial inventory levels reach a low of 2.6 billion in Sep2026, which would be the lowest level since April 2014. Global strategic stockpiling and the rebuild of oil on water imply a just over 20% share of landed OECD commercial stocks in global inventory increases in 2027 (below the historical 1/3 average but higher than the 10% in 2025). We forecast that the Hormuz shock and lingering uncertainty will cause faster strategic stock building from 2027 because end-2026 reserves will be low and because countries are likely to raise SPR targets. Our take was that Scenario B aligns with a prolonged hold, albeit with a tightening bias. This, we think, was validated by subsequent communication by Governor Bailey, and external members Taylor and Greene. As we see it, the forward-looking Taylor rule that we think Bailey and Taylor place a high weight on, suggests ~25bp delta between what is implied for the Bank Rate, on average, over the forecast horizon in the April MPR vs. the February MPR. records.text: 11 June 2026 Asia Local Markets Weekly Page 12 Deutsche Bank AG/Singapore Indonesia BI increases net yield on SRBIs, will offshore bite? Following the surprise 25bp hike by Bank Indonesia on 9 June, and their commitment to adjust the interest rate term structure for short-dated papers, the 12M SRBI was issued on 10 June at a weighted average yield of 7.57%, or 32bp higher than the last auction on 5 June. With a 12M onshore FX implied yield of ~6.55%, this would give an offshore FX hedged return of ~100bp, or almost 60bp higher than that observed at the last auction. Together with the 10% discount announced by Bank Indonesia on the FX swap premium, worth around 45pips at current levels, the cost of hedging should be further reduced by ~25bp, bringing the effective yield pick up on 12M SRBI to close to 125bp (not accounting for taxes or leverage costs etc). Will offshore investors respond with increasing their purchases of SRBIs? Looking back at 2024, during May-August of that year, when the FX implied 12M SRBI yielded a pickup of 116bp on average, we saw $3bn in monthly net buying of SRBIs by offshore investors. For context, offshore net bought $1bn per month of SRBIs between Jan-May this year, bringing ytd net inflows to around $5bn. The math should work in favour of more inflows. Whether that proves anything more than a circuit breaker for IDR – note that this flow does not add to spot dollar selling, but only to pool of onshore dollar liquidity – remains to be seen. Figure

records.text: Weaker Demand Offsets a Longer Hormuz Disruption Spot Brent futures have declined around 25% from the late March peak despite still low flows through Hormuz mainly for two reasons. First, on the physical side, the global oil market deficit during the disruption has been less large than expected. Second, on the financial side, investor positioning has moderated as market concerns about major escalation and large damage to production capacity have eased since the “ceasefire” (Exhibit 1). In this Oil Analyst, we keep our 2026Q4 Brent $90 price forecast because the easing effect from a smaller-than-expected deficit during the Hormuz disruption so far offsets the tightening effect from a longer disruption (Exhibit 2). We lower our 2027 average Brent forecast by $5 to $80 on higher supply and lower demand. records.text: 12 June 2026 Japan Economic Notes Page 2 Deutsche Securities Inc. A closer examination of the composition of these government-held assets is warranted. The most significant increase has occurred in foreign securities investment, which mainly consists of government-held foreign exchange reserves and foreign assets held by public pension funds like the Government Pension Investment Fund (GPIF). The assets at public pension funds underpin liabilities with a clearly defined use, i.e., future pension payouts, so it is inappropriate to simply subtract this from gross debt as proof of fiscal soundness. If this is to be excluded from the debt, then the discounted present value of future pension payments should also be included. Another concern is that a large portion of the government’s overseas assets is unhedged against currency fluctuations. Consequently, as the yen weakens, their yen-denominated valuation rises, reducing the net debt. The recent decline in the net debt ratio is largely due to the effect of these unrealized gains from the depressed yen. In fact, net debt excluding these overseas securities investments still exceeds levels prevailing before the global financial crisis. Under this structure, we believe that the emphasis by the government and ruling party on the importance of net debt signals implicitly to the markets that they accept, or even desire, a weaker yen, potentially heightening the risk of further yen depreciation. It is difficult for all of us to think on a non-linear basis, and we notice that there is not enough focus on extrapolating the implications of AI adoption over time. While it may sound daunting for LLM developers to accumulate 10x the compute to achieve a 2x increase in capabilities, an important mitigant is the rapid improvement in GPU and TPU computational power per chip. For example, for NVIDIA, we project that each new chip generation will have 250% more exaFLOPs, with only 60% more power usage. For a tracker of AI training facilities, see the EpochAI tracker here. The other element of the 10x:2x math that is not fully appreciated is the magnitude of importance relating to the doubling of model capabilities. Given that frontier LLMs can currently perform >50% of a wide range of human knowledge tasks at or better than humans (see analysis here), what might the economic implications be of a LLM that is twice as capable as the current best LLM? While difficult to determine precisely, we believe it is likely that, over time, the vast majority of knowledge tasks could be performed by frontier LLMs at or better than humans. records.text: 2 Euro Area Watch | 11 June 2026 Rates: relief rally in rates The rates market rallied on the back of the ECB’s press conference. President Lagarde repeated her analysis on the different types of energy price shocks and the differences in response they necessitate (look through, measured, forceful). Her emphasis on “measured” being the right response left the market reassured that the three hikes currently priced are likely a maximum. Lagarde also flagged the rather optimistic wage growth assumptions underpinning the ECB’s forecasts, which also suggest that the chance of cuts in 2027 may be higher than previously priced. The money market curve inverted slightly further, and Bunds outperformed USTs, in line with our view. EUR: limited impact, measured would be good The ECB meeting’s EUR impact was limited, with the FX price also somewhat affected by Iran headlines and the US PPI numbers. Most clients perceive ECB hikes as either risk management or a policy mistake, which has been in line with the downward move in belly real rates since the start of the war. Balanced guidance and a measured response would be the “sweet spot” for the EUR. In the near term and beyond the ECB, we maintain a bearish EUR bias (vs. USD and GBP), viewing energy futures as overly optimistic and expecting Euro area data to remain weak over the summer. FCNR(B) deposits are fixed-term bank deposits that can be opened in India by NRIs, OCIs, and PIOs. The facility will be available until 16 October 2026, for deposits mobilized by 30 September. We think this could save banks about 300bp of hedging costs in our view and allow them to offer significantly higher interest rates on 3-to-5-year foreign currency deposits. To facilitate this, the RBI has exempted these deposits from the Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio requirements. It has also relaxed rules to allow Indian banks to issue Standby Letters of Credit, enabling overseas banks to lend money to NRIs against their FCNR(B) deposits, which should create investment leverage opportunities. Prior to the announcement, three-year USD-denominated FCNR(B) deposits were offering interest rates in the range of 3.5–4%. With the new scheme these rates could increase to 6-7%, we think, pushing potential returns into the double digits with the addition of leverage. In 2013, a similar scheme resulted in inflows of about USD30bn over time (see Figure 1). records.text: Morgan Stanley Research; chart made at 09:00 London time, June 12th Second-round effects | It's…complicated: Waiting for second-round effects to emerge before tightening policy inevitably means acting too late. Hence, policy action is warranted when the risks of second-round effects are deemed sufficiently high. So what has happened since April on this front? The totality of evidence is, we would say, mixed. On the one hand, the Strait of Hormuz is still - at the time of writing - closed. If Scenario C remains as likely as was the case in April, and Scenario A is less likely, then any probability-weighted energy inflation path that MPC members assumed in April, is probably a bit higher now. Needless to say, if by the meeting next week, the traffic in the Strait of Hormuz does pick up, the opposite conclusion stands. In any case, barring material developments in the days ahead, we would place a bit more weight on a likely higher, not lower probability-weighted energy inflation path as anticipated by the median MPC member. Higher headline inflation does mean a higher risk of second-round effects, particularly in a framework where these are exclusively a result of higher inflation expectations, almost irrespective of the slack in the economy. This, we think, is why external member Greene will vote for a rate hike next week. The resulting mismatch between FX assets and liabilities within the banking system makes the EURCZK cross-currency basis sensitive to shifts in domestic EUR deposit funding. The FX loan-to-deposit ratio has stabilised around 130% (the midpoint of its range since 2015), suggesting the system is neither acutely short nor long EUR funding. More importantly, the composition of EUR deposits has shifted materially since the ECB lifted rates from the zero lower bound in mid-2022: the share of term deposits (as opposed to demand deposits) has risen significantly (Figure 1). This matters because term deposits provide a more stable funding base for FX loans, reducing the need for Czech banks to supplement funding via FX swaps and in turn curbing structural receiving pressure in xccy basis. Quarterly volatility: We share the ECB’s view on the main drivers weighing on growth, but these pressures do not seem fully reflected in the quarterly profile. The ECB still has GDP growth at 0.2% qoq in Q1, Q2 and Q3, followed by an acceleration to around potential and above from Q4 onwards. Admittedly, the ECB acknowledges that the signal from Q2 is softer than embedded in the projections. The explanation is that the projections include a potential rebound in Irish GDP, which could lift Q2 Euro Area growth after the sharp fall in Ireland in Q1. However, the ECB does not appear to incorporate the downward revision to Q1 euro area GDP, from +0.1% qoq initially reported to -0.2% qoq. As a result, Q2 could still come in line with the ECB projection if Ireland rebounds, but Q1 will inevitably be revised down in September ECB staff projections. Keeping the subsequent quarters in line with the ECB’s quarterly projections, the weaker Q1 starting point would leave 2026 growth closer to 0.4–0.5%, roughly half of the ECB’s published baseline. ECB Watching A robust hike The ECB delivered a 25bp hike and made clear that the decision was supported across a range of scenarios. With no forward guidance provided, a July move would require a material worsening in the energy backdrop. We continue to expect a second 25bp hike in September. Key decisions and takeaways Policy decision: As expected, the ECB Governing Council (GC) unanimously decided to raise all three policy rates by 25bp, bringing the deposit facility rate to 2.25%. Robust decision across scenarios: The decision was considered appropriate not only under the baseline scenario, but also under the alternative scenarios, including a milder one that assumes a faster normalisation in oil prices and a more rapid moderation in inflation. Not deemed an insurance hike...: The President declined to frame the decision as pre-emptive or as an insurance hike. Instead, she explained that it was a sound decision in response to a major energy shock that has lasted longer than experts had anticipated and is now beginning to feed more broadly into inflation. This includes the inevitable direct effects, but also indirect effects, while other consequences — including second-round effects — still need to be monitored. ...nor the start of a tightening cycle...: The President also refused to present the decision as the start of a tightening cycle, given the elevated uncertainty. Retail issuance is also performing well. Downgrade is not the base case, but complacency is not warranted Stronger fiscal execution has helped cushion the ratings, but it is not enough on its own to shift the outlook, in our view. Market access, stable financing, and continued recovery program implementation are all important positive signals, but a removal of negative outlooks is unlikely in the near term. records.text: Global Oil Fundamentals11 June 2026 ab 2 Global Oil Fundamentals UBS Research Oil price update: clock still ticking, more slowly With this note, we update our base case and scenario analysis and address key questions. Our base case sees prices stay close to current levels, in the $90s/bbl, through the rest of 2Q, as a potential peace deal keeps prices in check. For 3Q, we raise our Brent forecast to $105/bbl from $85/bbl with prices potentially climbing toward $120+/bbl ahead of the Hormuz reopening in the later part of July. This reflects the fact that we should be approaching more critical inventory levels, driving further demand reduction. We also raise our 4Q forecast to $90/bbl from $80/bbl, which raises the 2026 average by about $7/bbl to $93/bbl. Extended Hormuz disruptions and deeper inventory draws are likely to keep price higher for longer in our view. For 2027, we raise the forecast by $5/ bbl to $85/bbl as storage will have to be refilled amid limited supply growth; 2028 remains unchanged at $75/bbl. We make a similar change to our WTI forecasts. Türkiye: Geopolitics delays disinflation, FX stability holds The tone on Türkiye was cautious, with the disinflation process increasingly challenged by geopolitical developments, even as the monetary stance remains tight in response to rising inflation risks. Higher oil prices linked to the Middle East conflict are feeding into energy and food inflation, pushing headline prints higher and weighing on expectations, with risks tilted to the upside amid potential second round effects. At the same time, moderating domestic demand and easing inertia across services subgroups suggest that disinflation could resume once the energy shock dissipates, albeit at a slower pace than envisaged pre-conflict. Georgia: strong fundamentals, but oil shock complicates the outlook Georgia remains a small, open BB-rated economy with a consistently business-friendly framework, underpinned by low taxation and strong growth dynamics. Rapid expansion has driven a doubling in GDP per capita over the past five years, reinforcing the country’s convergence story and investor appeal. Middle East – North Africa (MENA): Iran war tremors The fog of the Iran war continues to cloud the economic outlook of the MENA region. But what matters for the market is the pricing for implied volatility for that date. Based on current pricing in the options market, it already appears that market participants are placing a multiple of 1.5 to 2 days worth of moves for the upcoming FOMC meeting (higher for shorter tenors). This is in line with what the historical pattern would suggest on a realized vol-adjusted basis. Further implied volatility over the next month is already priced to be higher than the realized volatility over the previous month, across the entire surface except for 5y and 10y tenors, and especially for 1y and 2y tenors. And our results for 10y tenor surprises for new Fed chairs are not especially strong. So the vol market is not obviously under-pricing a potential Warsh surprise. Yet in neither case was the market able to sustain such elevated volatility. Instead, realized volatility exhibited a recurring pattern: roughly every seven weeks, 21-day realized volatility retraced toward pre-conflict norms ( Exhibit 5 ). While the sample size is limited, the similarity suggests that while the rates market can quickly incorporate geopolitical shocks into prices, it struggles to maintain an elevated level of volatility over a multi-month period. Implied volatility has followed a similarly consistent path. Although realized volatility normalized, ongoing geopolitical uncertainty prevented a comparable decline in option premiums ( Exhibit 6 ). At this point into both conflicts, 1y2y implied volatility remained roughly 20bp/year above pre-conflict levels, highlighting investors' continued willingness to pay for protection.

records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 and softer in second half, it also introduces seasonality into TIPS yields (Exhibit 5 ) . Without adjusting for this effect, some of the apparent richness or cheapness in the TIPS curve may simply reflect CPI seasonality. We therefore seasonally adjust the clean price of each TIPS bond and convert that adjusted price back into SA yields (Exhibit 6 ). For this adjustment, we use the multiplicative seasonal factors released by the BLS. Ideally, we would price TIPS using a TIPS zero-coupon curve, similar to the approach used for Treasuries. We tested different combinations of knot points, weights, and interpolators, but the results were not stable enough through time. The main challenge is that the TIPS universe is much smaller, especially in the front end, so the constructed curve is less consistent across dates. To get a seasonally adjusted TIPS curve, we fit a Nelson Siegel curve through the seasonally adjusted TIPS yields. This is not the ideal way to do this but it gives us a good approximation. In case of TIPS, we measure the deviation of the bond as a difference directly from the spline ( Exhibit 8 ). This is different than the way we do it for Treasuries which is market yield minus curve implied model yield. records.text: European Rates Weekly 12 June 2026 Citi Research 6 Demand-driven framework of liquidity provision still on paper only. With the bulk of short-dated bond financing taking place at or below depo, demand for the ECB’s standard credit facilities (serving refi) has remained lukewarm at best (Figure 6), making up a negligible share of total bank liabilities (1.3% as of end-April). In other words, the bulk of outstanding liquidity is still a legacy of the years of QE profligacy, making the transition to the demand-driven framework of liquidity provision a still distant signpost. Even when demand for liquidity at refi eventually picks up, however, we are wary of interpreting it as impacting the transmission of monetary policy—over the post-TLTRO.III years, usage of central + regional government paper has averaged less than 2% of the eligible stock (Figure 7), meaning that even in years of lukewarm appetite for direct ECB financing, liquidity transformation (i.e., the tendency of ECB counterparties to mobilize non-HQLA collateral to secure reserves against it) has continued being a key feature of the liquidity management of EA banks. We therefore expect the ultimate sustained increase in appetite for ECB cash to precede cheaper repo rates, which remain our preferred early-warning indicator that the jurisdictions with “spare” excess liquidity have reached their target level of reserves. records.text: Given the recent upside surprises in the labor data, we are upgrading our labor market forecasts modestly. Our payroll averages for 2026 and 2027 are now 82k (previous: 45k) and 69k (previous: 43k). Our new payroll trajectory accounts for the impact of the World Cup and summer weakness in hiring. Recent Q2 data remain firm, with both households and firms performing well. Household consumption is supported by real wage growth above 1% amid low inflation. Corporate sentiment also appears resilient. The latest Business Outlook Survey suggests improved sentiment in Q2 despite Middle East uncertainties, and the June Tankan DI for large firms may show only a limited decline. We therefore expect Q2 GDP growth to slow but remain solid at an annualized +1.3%, somewhat above consensus. Private consumption should stay firm, and capex may also remain steady (see latter). We revise our FY2026 growth forecast up to 0.8% (from 0.7%), above the BoJ’s 0.5% projection. We also bring forward the impact of the food VAT cut (to 1%) from October 2027 to April 2027, raising FY2027 growth to 1.2% (from 1.1%), while lowering FY2028 to 0.8% (from 1.0%). Entering a more sustained upcycle? Despite the global AI boom, Japan’s capex has increased at a relatively modest pace, with real growth of 1.1%YoY versus 5.7% in the U.S. However, it may be premature to conclude that Japan is missing out on the AI investment cycle. Machine tool orders—a leading indicator of manufacturing capex—show that while growth has been driven by external demand, domestic demand is now entering a clear recovery phase ( link).
