records.text: M Idea 10 Rates Strategy: MPC Risks Tilt Marginally Hawkish Fabio Bassanin In our base case, we expect a 7–2 vote split in favour of a hike and see mildly hawkish risks going into the meeting. The key reason behind this bias is that the MPC has not received the benign geopolitical resolution it may have hoped for in April. The US–Iran conflict remains unresolved and a swift normalization has yet to materialize. In the our view, for the MPC this likely reduces the probability of Scenario A relative to April and increases the weight attached to Scenarios B and C. That said, the tone of the meeting could still be affected by near-term geopolitical developments. As things stand, the situation remains highly fluid, with recent headlines suggesting that a US–Iran agreement could be reached as soon as this weekend. These reports have already supported a more optimistic market reaction, lowering hiking expectations and driving a rally in front-end rates. Should a formal agreement be reached ahead of the MPC meeting, the risk of a hawkish message would likely diminish. For now, however, uncertainty remains elevated. Admittedly, energy prices are not validating the most adverse outcome. Oil prices remain broadly between the assumptions underlying Scenarios A and B, rather than moving decisively towards Scenario C. Structurally, investor concerns centre on embedded legal features that can disadvantage bondholders, including early termination rights, and the ability of counterparties to enforce claims ahead of a restructuring. This creates risks around effective priority, pre- emptive exit, and comparability of treatment, especially if counterparties extract near- full recovery. Institutional scrutiny is increasing, with multilateral institutions and rating agencies in the process of formalising their frameworks, but sentiment suggests these instruments are unlikely to be viewed favourably. The message from investors is that any form of subordination, particularly in distress scenarios, is viewed negatively given its direct impact on recovery values. Resource-backed financing is also typically viewed by investors as effectively super- senior, given their reliance on ring-fenced commodity revenues and escrow structures that prioritise repayment ahead of other creditors. This creates a direct constraint on fiscal flexibility, particularly when commodity prices reverse, as a significant share of revenue is pre-committed and cannot be redeployed to absorb shocks. records.text: Japan Economy Policy rates headed back to 1% for first time since 1995 We expect the BoJ to raise rates next week, emphasizing upside inflation risks over downside economic risks, then to 1.5% by next spring. In the interim assessment of QT , a halt to the reduction in JGB purchases is expected from FY27 onward. BoJ preview (June 2026): Policy rates headed back to 1% for first time since 1995 This is an update of BoJ preview (June 2026): Policy rates headed back to 1% for first time since 1995, 10 June 2026. At the monetary policy meeting (MPM) to be held on 15-16 June, we expect the BoJ to raise the policy rate from the current 0.75% to 1%, the highest level since 1995. As of the January MPM, we had sensed that concerns within the BoJ Policy Board about JPY depreciation stemming from the exceptionally low real policy rate had risen markedly, and we had therefore expected a rate hike at the April meeting. However, at the time of that meeting, uncertainty surrounding the Middle East situation was extremely high, leaving the BoJ little choice but to wait and see. Into June, however, the process toward agreement has continued, albeit with twists and turns along the way, and the absence of major downward pressure on production and consumption has also been confirmed. We therefore think the BoJ will conclude that it should go ahead with a rate hike without waiting for the July Outlook Report, placing greater weight on its commitment to addressing upside inflation risks. These include: (1) deposit outflows to major and online banks driven by demographic fac- tors, which may shorten duration estimates independently of monetary policy; (2) declining stickiness of ordinary deposits, as yields lag those of time deposits and money reserve funds (MRFs) as rate hikes proceed; and (3) the possibility that deposit rate pass-through rises with further rate hikes. All of these act to further shorten the duration of core deposits. Even regional financial institutions, which tend to have a strong preference for carry, are finding it increasingly difficult to build duration positions. In addition, as rate hikes widen the gap between market rates and ordinary deposit rates, both major banks and regional financial institutions are able to secure sufficient margins even through current account-based asset management. records.text: M Idea 4 the market yield and the model-implied yield for the input bonds. At each iteration, we calculate the sum of error of market and model implied yields and try to minimize it. The number and placement of knot points determine the degrees of freedom of the curve, meaning it controls how tightly fit the curve can be. The weights determine how much importance each bond has in the fitting process. A higher weight means the optimizer will try harder to fit that bond closely. More knot points make the curve more flexible and allow it to fit the bond inputs more closely. Fewer knot points produce a smoother curve. After getting the zero-coupon curve (MSUSSY10 Index), we can derive the par rate of a bond which is the coupon rate that would make a hypothetical Treasury trade at its face value ( Exhibit 3 ). This par curve closely tracks the yield to maturities of all the bonds. We calculate the curve-implied yield of each bond based on its cash flows using the zero coupon curve ( Exhibit 4 ). The difference between the market yield and the curve-implied yield determines whether a bond is rich or cheap. We upload the sum of this absolute average difference for a day as MSTVI Index on bloomberg which is in basis points terms. If the market yield is higher than the curve-implied yield, the bond is cheap and vice-versa. Some CUSIPs can remain rich or cheap versus the curve-implied yield for a long period because of liquidity, on-the-run/off-the-run status or other technical factors

India and Indonesia have faced parallel challenges over the past few months as their currencies depreciated rapidly against the dollar. Year-to-date, the rupee is 6.1% lower, while the rupiah has fallen 7.2%. In response, both central banks announced measures last week designed to support their respective currencies. This note addresses key client questions related to these measures and their potential impact on the markets. Q1. What measures did the RBI announce? INR depreciation pressure has reflected capital outflows from equities, exacerbated by a current account balance that has deteriorated on the back of higher oil prices and a decline in the Indian IT sector amid the global rise of AI technology. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has responded with the measures set out below – we expect the FCNR and external commercial borrowings initiatives to have the most significant impact on the currency. Attractive FCNR(B) deposits: The RBI will fully cover the FX hedging costs for banks that raise fresh 3-to-5- year Foreign Currency Non-Resident deposits (known as (FCNR(B) deposits) . r that the jurisdictions with “spare” excess liquidity have reached their target level of reserves. Beware of autonomous liquidity factors. At the current pace of APP and PEPP redemptions (available for the next two years here and here, respectively), excess liquidity should reach the €2tn handle at the beginning of 2027, with the key source of uncertainty represented by the projected evolution of the so-called autonomous factors. Since the last TLTRO.III repayments, these have accounted for 20% of the decrease in the size of the monetary policy portfolios, which infers that, against €1 of passive QT, excess liquidity has declined by €0.80 on average. However, the impact of autonomous factors is not just a matter of delta but of levels as well. As the ECB’s balance sheet continues to shrink, the ability of the stock of reserves to cover fluctuations in the likes of banknotes in circulation or €- denominated non-monetary policy deposits diminishes. Possibly before the demand-driven framework is in full swing (meaning that the marginal unit of liquidity is provided at refi via the ECB’s standard liquidity facilities), it may very well be that deviations from the structural trend in autonomous factors will have the power to impact € money markets—similarly to the role played by the TGA rebuild on the level of reserves at the Fed and on $ money markets in summer 2025. records.text: 11 June 2026 Asia Local Markets Weekly Page 14 Deutsche Bank AG/Singapore Vietnam Shifting tides - from stability to weakness YTD, the Dong has been a regional outperformer, holding flat against the US dollar. The currency remained resilient even following the escalation of US-Iran tensions in March, weakening only ~1%. This stability was attributed to three key factors: first, active smoothing in the FX market by SBV; second, strong FDI inflows, which at ~$9.8bn YTD are the highest on record for this period; and third, a healthy trade surplus that persisted until late last year. However, this supportive picture is now shifting. For the first time since the COVID- 19 disruptions of 2021—and before that, 2016—Vietnam is recording a widening monthly trade deficit. The YTD trade deficit now stands at ~$13bn, a sharp reversal from the $5bn surplus recorded during the same period in 2025. This deterioration is driven by three main forces: n Strong domestic consumption. Retail sales are growing at an average of 11% year-to-date, the fastest pace since 2023. In May, retail goods accounted for 76% of total sales and grew 11.1% YoY, fueling a sharp rise in imports, particularly electronics. n Higher commodity costs. Rising commodity prices, especially for fuel, are adding to import pressures. Oil prices have increased by approximately 32% YoY since the start of the US-Iran conflict. n Persistent 'hot money' outflows . Our analysis suggests an increase in capital outflows. This is evid

Dealer positioning could amplify realized volatility Based on swaption trades reported to the SDR, we infer customer flows in the OTC swaptions market. Using this information, we estimate dealers' aggregate net gamma exposure from outstanding swaptions. Since the SDR reporting standard was updated in January 2024, dealer net gamma exposure has not previously turned negative (Exhibit 8 ). Assuming dealers actively hedge their delta exposure, negative gamma implies that aggregate dealer hedging flows tend to reinforce market moves (at least locally, see Exhibit 7 ), contributing to higher realized volatility. Conversely, when dealers are net long gamma, hedging flows tend to lean against market moves, dampening directional price action and reducing realized volatility.

records.text: US Economics Weekly12 June 2026 ab 8 Annual trade revisions to boost Q1 GDP The BEA’s annual trade revision narrowed the goods and services deficit by about 3.2% on average from 1999 through 2024, but it left a different contour in the latest data: the 2025 deficit was revised 2.2% wider, while the Q1 2026 deficit was revised 4.1% narrower. The revisions reflect updated goods source data, BOP adjustments, reclassifications, recalculated seasonal factors, and more substantial updates to services trade, including new BEA survey data and improved estimates of transport services. The services revisions were the larger driver and in March the level of services imports were revised down 2.8%, compared with a 1.2% downward revision to goods imports, while goods exports were little changed and services exports were revised down 1.1%. For GDP , the wider 2025 deficit points to a weaker net-export contribution last year, but the narrower Q1 deficit should boost the third estimate of Q1 growth. BEA will incorporate the revised Q1 trade data on a best-change basis in the June 25 third estimate, while leaving Q4 unrevised; the full history will not flow through the national accounts until the September NIPA annual revision. We estimate that net exports now contributed -0.4pp to Q1 GDP growth, versus -1.3pp in BEA’s second estimate. See the forecast table on page 28. Once the market normalises, the next key question is how quickly inventories can be replenished. Let's move now to the policy aspect of that discussion: does any of the above matter? After all, this is well identified and the ECB projections are very transparent on the impact of Ireland. The easy fix for policymakers would be to focus on EA numbers excluding Ireland. But can policymakers really forget about headline figures? Let's imagine two scenarios here. Assume first that we are right and Irish GDP does not rebound in 2Q26. In September, the ECB projections will have to take on board much lower EA growth numbers in the first half of 2026, and its forecasts of 2026 growth would fall mechanically towards 0.4%Y. For example, for an item whose price has risen particularly sharply since the previous base year, Pi/P is greater than 1, but when the base is revised, this returns to roughly 1 (Figure 4). If this item maintains a high inflation rate, rebasing reduces its weight, exerting downward pressure on the y/y rate of CPI (Figure 3). Moreover, items whose prices have fallen sharply since the previous base year can also be a factor behind downward revisions. Such items have Pi/P below 1, but rebasing raises this to 1, restoring their weight. If this item’s inflation rate remains low, this also pushes down CPI. records.text: Global Oil Fundamentals11 June 2026 ab 11 2) What is the extent of the supply disruption? The ongoing Hormuz disruptions have forced significant oil production supply shut-ins in the Gulf and the situation got worse between late March and today. We estimate that total liquids supply losses reached ~15Mb/d in May, up from nearly 12Mb/d in March and nearly14Mb/d in April. We estimate that Iran drove most of the reduction, down 1.3Mb/d to 2.2Mb/d, as its exports fell sharply from 1.5Mb/d in April to just 260kb/d in May under the US naval blockade. We expect the disruption to stabilise close to current levels as some extra UAE production is offset by lower Iranian production. There may be some further production upside if dark transits persist close to levels seen month to date but this would only represent an extra ~1Mb/d. records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 12 Jun 2026 12:44:20 ET │ 21 pages US Economics Labor Market Update: May 2026 CITI'S TAKE Payroll employment data have clearly picked up over the last three months, averaging 188k/month from March through May compared to -4k over the three months before. But a reacceleration in labor demand is not echoed in other data. We see more evidence in leading indicators like very low hiring plans that stronger job growth reflects a temporary increase in employment levels rather than a sustained strengthening in demand for workers. Most notably, the unemployment rate has remained stable at 4.3% despite stronger payroll job growth and large declines in labor force participation (due partly to older workers, which we dig into a bit more here). We continue to expect that job growth through the end of the year will have averaged a bit below the breakeven rate that would keep unemployment steady and continue to expect rising unemployment over the summer. Rates Fixed Income Blog Date 12 June 2026 ECB: this is not 2011 Hiking in response to a negative supply shock is, by definition, uncomfortable. This is leading some to conclude that the ECB is repeating the policy mistake of 2011. However, the comparison with 2011 is misplaced for three fundamental reasons. Firstly, the private sector is more resilient than in the aftermath of the GFC. Secondly, intra -EU divergences are smaller, as peripheral countries have significantly improved their external positions. Thirdly, on a forward-looking basis, fiscal policy is likely to ease rather than tighten, as it did post-2011. Back in 2011, the ECB tightened monetary policy in response to the negative supply shock triggered by the Arab Spring, which led to higher oil prices. Within six months, the ECB had to reverse course. Ultimately, the easing cycle ended with negative intere st rates and large -scale QE. While the parallel with 2011 is appealing, it is unlikely to hold, as both initial conditions and forward -looking dynamics are materially different. Market pric- ing for the year (~25bp) is at the lower end of the range in our view and has room for upside as even if the conflict ends, the ex-ante inflation picture already arguably warranted hikes. Meanwhile, Riksbank risks skew dovish; our economics expect a shift towards a tightening bias signalling the possi- bility of a hike this year, but this is already more-than-priced by rates markets (30bp by year-end). Given inflation and growth are running substantially below forecasts, it will be difficult for the central bank to out-hawk market pricing. To do so, they would need to either signal several hikes or indi- cate that the hawkish alternative scenario — which assumes three hikes and which "envisages a lengthy closure of the Strait, and one that produces inflation pressures on commodi- ties beyond energy; the currency falls and unemployment ris- es” — is becoming the baseline . If the Riksbank were to sur- prise hawkishly, SEK may benefit tactically, but we don’t expect this to be long-lasting or change the big picture for the currency as other factors are still unsupportive (low carry in global context amid even higher yields abroad, equity momentum, regional growth/fiscal). records.text: ab 12 June 2026 Global Research Japan Macro Watch Rate hike amid firmer economic conditions BoJ set to raise rates to 1% We expect the BoJ to raise the policy rate from 0.75% to 1.0% at the June 15–16 policy meeting, in line with the consensus view. Governor Ueda’s hawkish remarks last week, along with a Nikkei report, point towards a rate hike. The move would signal that the BoJ is prioritizing upside inflation risks over downside growth risks. The BoJ is also expected to halt further reductions in JGB purchases from next April, maintaining purchases at ¥2.1 trillion per month. Governor Ueda is expected to miss the meeting due to illness, with Deputy Governor Himino chairing and Deputy Governor Uchida handling the press conference. Neither is likely to display a strong hawkish or dovish bias relative to Ueda. With BEI now above 2%, the BoJ faces increasing pressure to maintain credibility in containing inflation and may emphasize a continued tightening bias. A BoJ watcher survey shows that around 60% see rising risks of the BoJ falling behind the curve. Otherwise, inflation expectations, BEI, and long-term yields could rise further. We expect a follow-up rate hike as early as October after June, assuming further upside in underlying and expected inflation. records.text: US Economics Weekly12 June 2026 ab 11 Overstatements in economic impact estimates are likely driven by three key mechanisms: substitution effects, crowding out, and leakage. Spending by domestic residents during the world cup may simply displace other forms of consumption rather than increase total economic activity, while congestion and high prices can deter regular tourists, offsetting gains from event-related visitors. A substantial share of tournament revenues flow to FIFA, reducing the portion retained within host economies. The world cup is also sometimes co-hosted, splitting the economic benefits among countries. Indeed, this year's world cup is co-hosted between the US, Canada and Mexico, though as noted above, 78 of the 104 matches and all of the games from the quarter finals onward will be hosted in the US. Current data for the 2026 world cup is thus far in line with our sense that it will lead to limited durable economic impact. Tourism Economics estimates incremental tourism — visitors who would not have come to the US without the world cup — to include as many as 1.2 million international visitors to US host cities specifically because of the tournament, with 60% classified as additional trips generated by the event (link here). More recent spring 2026 reporting references ~1.5 million visitors, so in the same ballpark (link here). FIFA, in estimates compiled with the WTO, estimates a total attendance of 3.7 million in the US, with roughly 40% coming from outside

records.text: Watch for JPY depreciation risk around Deputy Governor Uchida's press conference Since the April MPM, many Policy Board members have laid the groundwork for a June rate hike In his 3 June speech, Governor Ueda avoided a “pre- commitment” but showed strong willingness to raise rates A strong warning on upside inflation risks, including behind- the-curve risk Inflation driven by higher oil prices and JPY depreciation is already emerging in B2B transactions we sense a risk to deletion at a time when expectations for a US rate hike are rising and JPY depreciation pressure is liable to intensify, and therefore expect the wording to be left unchanged this time around. The nature of the drop has been different though as China reduced imports. OECD commercial inventories have not come down as materially as could be feared. US commercial inventories have been declining at ~1Mb/d though and could approach very low levels by the end of July, forcing greater demand adjustments by then.  How quickly will production come back once the Strait reopens? The return of production would not be immediate as it would likely take 2-3 weeks to get enough tankers back into the region for the onshore storage to start being drained. Some countries could restart production within days and others within a few weeks. Overall, we estimate that ~2/3 of lost supply should be back on stream within 3 months of the Strait reopening and >90% would be back within 6 months. We model only limited permanent loss of production capacity.  How long will it take for inventories to rebuild? We estimate that we will have lost close to 3bn bbls of liquids on a gross basis by the time production returns to normal, assuming a reopening this summer. On a net basis, adjusted for lower demand, this could still be close to 1.5bn bbls. Assuming a pace of 2Mb/d inventory rebuild, it would take 2 years to return to previous levels. We believe there could be extra "demand" to build higher strategic reserves post conflict, adding to it.

A win for Labour candidate Andy Burnham was seen as the marginal base case by our speakers, which, if it materializes, would imply a high chance of him becoming the next Labour leader. The view among speakers was that any potential new Labour leader is unlikely to make major changes to fiscal rules or break manifesto commitments on tax, at least in the near term. But some highlighted risks of future changes to the debt rule to allow for more investment. Public private partnerships, tax reform, investment in social care and sectoral taxes are all potential policy choices that could be adopted if there were to be a left-leaning Labour leader. Longer term, a shift towards a closer UK-EU relationship would need to be politically credible for both businesses and the EU to engage.

This time, he cited a need to “thoroughly discuss” whether to raise rates. records.text: 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa Distributed on: 12/06/2026 06:33:14 GMT Distributed on: 12/06/2026 06:33:14 GMT 12 June 2026 Chart of the week: Government/LDP’s focus on net debt On June 9, a Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) working group on responsible fiscal policy submitted a proposal to Economic and Fiscal Policy Minister Minoru Kiuchi. The proposal advocates for the elimination of the consumption tax on food. We have already addressed the issues with reducing the consumption tax in our January report and will not revisit those arguments here. Our concern this time is the group's call to use multiple indicators in addition to gross debt, such as “net debt,” to assess the fiscal situation. While this sounds reasonable, we believe an undue emphasis on net debt is problematic. Our calculations suggest that Japan’s general government net debt (total debt minus government-held assets like stocks, bonds and deposits) dropped to 66% of GDP as of end-2025, the lowest level since 2007 (just prior to the global financial crisis). This figure stands in stark contrast to the nation’s debt-to-GDP ratio of 207%. That 141-percentage-point gap represents the financial assets held by the government. Rates: Rising yields would reduce the value of fixed- income assets, leading to lower pension capital. However, given that interest -rate risk is not fully hedged (Figure 5), even with this smaller pot of pension capital, a larger theoretical future annuity at retirement can be achieved due to higher yields. As this larger theoretical annuity has more interest-rate risk, more interest rate hedges would be required. Therefore, (slightly counterintuitively) we expect higher yields to lead to increased interest-rate hedging (via swap receiving or bond buying, or both) under the solidarity contract. A fall in yields would have the opposite impact, leading to swap paying and bond selling , in our view. For the return portfolio, we believe that the lower pension capital from rising yields would lead pension funds to rebalance by selling equities, the corollary of which is that declining yields would lead to higher pension capital and equity buying. records.text: BNY inflation expectations ease lower in May Median three-year inflation expectations in the FRBNY Survey of Consumer Expectations fell 0.1 pp in the rounding to 3.1% in May, following 0.1 pp increases in both March and April. Unrounded, the measure edged down 0.02 pp to 3.13%. Prior to the conflict, expectations at the three-year horizon were firm at 3.0% for five straight months. At the five-year horizon, a shorter time series, inflation expectations were unchanged at 3.0% in May. Overall, this survey suggests that inflation expectations remain well-anchored. One-year ahead inflation expectations can be sensitive to changes in gasoline prices, and the US average all-grade retail gasoline price rose to $4.61 at the end of May, up from $3.07 at the end of February. Despite the elevated level, one-year ahead inflation expectations fell 0.1 pp to 3.5% in May, now 0.5 pp above the February level prior to the conflict. Gas price expectations also eased slightly. The year-ahead gas price change expectation fell 0.1 pp to 5.0% in May, remaining well above the 3.7% average in the 12 months prior to the conflict and the 2.7% level in May a year ago. However the FOMC has not hit their target in five years and that concern is fairly widespread across the FOMC. They would like to see evidence inflation is headed back toward 2%. In April 2025 headline inflation had fallen to 2.3% and core PCE inflation had fallen to 2.6% with favorable forward indicators in components of shelter inflation. Scheme choices within new pension system: Transitioning funds can choose between two types of new pension schemes: flexible contract or solidarity contract. The flexible contract type operates somewhat like a classic defined contribution scheme, with individuals having control over their investment allocation. Under the solidarity contract, investments follow a lifecycle approach, with younger participants invested mostly in riskier assets, which are gradually reduced as retirement approaches. Investment choices here are left to the PF manager, with individuals unable to directly influence their investment mix. The solidarity contract has been the industry’s dominant choice, with over 90% of Dutch PFs’ assets under management transitioning to this type of scheme. As the flexible contract shows a greater deviation from the old pension system, we think funds transitioning to this type of scheme will likely require larger hedging adjustments. However, post-transition, the solidarity scheme may offer more interest for market participants, with regular asset- mix rebalancing likely. Hence, the solidarity scheme is the focus of our analysis . records.text: European Rates Weekly 12 June 2026 Citi Research 11 UK: one day, two votes The MPC and Makerfield both vote on 18 June. The MPC looks set to remain on hold for the coming meetings (with the ECB more likely to hike in July than the MPC in our view). We expect the argument that it has already tightened to trump hawkish calls to be preemptive. Slowly fading hike premium could combine with growing fiscal risk into the autumn (we look at various scenarios post-Makerfield) for a steeper 2s10s gilt curve: we target 100bp by year-end. The Bank vs the by-election. The coincidence of the MPC meeting and the Makerfield by-election on 18 June is reflective of the two most influential drivers of gilts at present, namely: (1) the influence on monetary policy from geopolitics; (2) the influence of domestic politics on fiscal policy. While neither events may have much immediate impact on market pricing, both could set the scene for H2, potentially combining to steepen the gilt curve over the medium term. BoE – action with inaction While the vote is taking place in Makerfield, the Bank is likely to be opting for action with inaction. The BoE looks set for another “active hold” in policy rates, albeit with a potential change to the vote split. A 7–2 vote (vs 8–1 in April, with Megan Greene most likely to join Huw Pill in dissenting) would not be a surprise to the market, but 6–3 onwards probably would be. records.text: 11 June 2026 Focus Europe Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 Not a ‘forceful’ tightening President Lagarde mentioned the reaction function she originally presented at the ECB Watchers’ conference in March and the three options the ECB has to respond to the energy shock. The ECB could ‘look through’ the shock if the impact on inflation was small and transitory, could implement a ‘measured’ tightening if the inflation shock was large but not too persistent and a ‘forceful or persistent’ tightening if the inflation shock was significant and sustained. By hiking in June, the ECB has decided that ‘look through’ is not a robust response. But, President Lagarde also said that today’s action was not a ‘forceful’ tightening either. There is danger of over-interpretation, but there are a couple of points to make about this. First, no one would consider a 25bp hike to be forceful in and of itself. But by putting it this way President Lagarde may have been hinting that the ECB sees itself in the ‘measured’ response, not the ‘forceful’ response. This will suit the doves. Second, by not repeating that the third option is a ‘forceful or persistent’ tightening (Lagarde only said ‘forceful’ today), was Lagarde hinting that a ‘persistent’ tightening is not an option and the real choice is ‘measured’ vs ‘forceful’? Maybe all Lagarde meant was that it is too soon to judge the persistence of the policy stance - in the first instance it is the scale of tightening that it needs to determine. Our takeaway Our

records.text: 2 Europe Economic Weekly | 12 June 2026 Weekly view One hike, more coming The ECB delivered its well-telegraphed hike this week. Also as expected, that came with no pre-commitment on the trajectory, a data-dependent approach, but still a nod that, absent very good news (on energy prices) or very bad news (on the economy), they’re not done here. Indeed, Lagarde took us back to the Watchers’ speech when she described three broad scenarios depending on the size and the persistence of the shock. And she implied that we are in a scenario that needs a measured response (not a forceful one). That, together with forecasts that include more than one hike, while still having inflation back at target, also signals they not done yet. That means a short hiking cycle, in line with our base case of two hikes, but a third one is possible if there are additional surprises in the data. Our (admittedly low-conviction) expectation is for another hike in July. The conclusion from today is that July is live, but the urgency generated by energy prices will dictate when we get there – otherwise they will deliver in September. We push back on the idea of the ECB doing a “one and done” or an “insurance” hike. Lagarde also pushed back against that this week. “One and done” is not unthinkable, but this is a scenario they would get to by accident, not something they have in mind today. records.text: Developments around the Strait of Hormuz, and their implications for energy prices, are likely to remain a key driver of euro area yields, particularly at the front end. The ECB has underscored its sensitivity to higher energy prices and the risk of indirect/second-round effects on inflation: it raised policy rates by 25bp at the June meeting and signaled a willing- ness to tighten further. While the staff forecasts are consistent with additional hikes, we expect one more 25bp increase in September, with risks skewed to more should energy pric- es remain elevated. Ultimately, the ECB’s ability to pause should depend on the depth and duration of the energy crisis while balancing its impact on inflation (upside) and growth (downside). Visibility around the full opening of the Strait remains limited, although recent developments around a potential agreement on the MOU point to some improvement. We continue to assess the implications for European rates using the scenario-analysis frame- work outlined previously. Our leg-by-leg forecast is as follows: we see SOFR averaging around -6bp versus IORB in July, while FF should decline by about 1bp, reflecting its response to soft repo conditions, similar to the sensitivity seen in May, leaving FF around -4bp. This implies a fair value level of +2bp for July SOFR/FF, with upside to +3bp if the funds rate proves stickier. We expect a bit firmer funding in the second half of June than the first half, which would provide an even more attractive entry versus current prices, as July pricing is likely to respond to changes in spot funding markets. For instance, The TGA is set to rise on Monday following tax payments and mid-month Treasury coupon settlements, which should lift SOFR back toward IORB. Given the above we recommend going long July SOFR/FF (entry -1.0bp) targeting a level of +2bp. records.text: Japan Macro Watch12 June 2026 ab 2 BoJ set to raise rates to 1% As noted in our BoJ preview memo , we expect the BoJ to raise the policy rate from 0.75% to 1.0% at next week’s meeting, in line with the consensus. This would be the first hike in six months, bringing the policy rate to its highest level since 1995. Governor Ueda’s hawkish remarks last week, combined with the Nikkei report, point towards a rate hike. The hike suggests the BoJ is prioritizing upside inflation risks over downside growth risks. Regarding the reduction in JGB purchases, market participants have been split on whether the BoJ would continue tapering beyond April 2027 or halt reductions. According to the same report, purchases are likely to be maintained at ¥2.1 trillion per month from April next year. Current monthly redemptions (~¥7 trillion) far exceed purchases, and our simulations suggest the BoJ’s JGB holdings could halve from the 2023 peak of ¥598 trillion to around ¥300 trillion by 2032. Given uncertainty over the private sector’s ability to absorb this supply, the BoJ is likely to emphasize flexibility, including the option to increase purchases if long-term yields rise sharply. Governor Ueda is expected to miss next week’s meeting due to illness; Deputy Governor Himino will chair, and Deputy Governor Uchida will handle the press conference. Indicators of inflationary pressures within surveys have risen, the currency has depreciated slightly more than expected, and energy prices moved further up from those in the March MPR. All Board members broadly agreed in the May meeting that risks of higher inflation have somewhat increased and that the favourable inflationary conditions could quickly become a thing of the past (see Minutes). Since then, the Governor reiterated his stance that the Middle East conflict is creating risks of potentially higher inflation further ahead (see Thedeen). Still, we do not expect a full rate hike to be priced in, given the large uncertainty and dependence of the path on the development of energy prices. At this stage, the Board is unlikely to fully endorse the need to tighten at one of the next meetings as uncertainty remains very high. However, we think that the Board will not be able to rule out that tightening could happen at one of the upcoming meetings. A change of stance is therefore needed from the current prolonged hold. In our view, a revision of the policy rate path, with a possible (but not certain) rate hike in 3Q, could be a compromise to keep all options on the table.

Japan: Solid wage momentum helps cushion future headwinds The preliminary April Monthly Labour Statistics suggest wage growth remained firm. Nominal wages rose to 3.5% yoy, while real wages stayed positive for a fourth consecutive month, at 1.9%, mainly driven by low inflation. Unlike in 2022-24, when bonuses were the main swing factor, base pay growth of around 2.5-3.0% is anchoring nominal wage gains now. A small change in the balance of risks Indeed, the balance of risks is shifting towards a third hike being more likely than “one and done.” For starters, one could argue that even in the mild scenario from the ECB, two hikes would still be needed to bring inflation back to target by the end of 2028. And, while above we argue that the adverse scenario could be seen as consistent with two hikes also, it’s not a clear case, and a third could be needed. More importantly, we would push back on the idea of the ECB doing a “one and done” or an “insurance” hike. records.text: Global Oil Fundamentals11 June 2026 ab 33 Global Oil Market UBS Scenario We expect Brent to remain in the $90s over the rest of 2Q26 as flows via Hormuz remain very disrupted but inventories cover the shortfall. As this diminishes over July, we expect prices to rise towards recent highs, leading to an agreement to reopen Hormuz. We believe that the market is likely to factor in a structurally higher risk premium though, as tensions are likely to linger. A limited supply response and the need to rebuild inventories should also support prices in 2027. Looking further out, rising efficiency and EVs' increasing impact should see demand growth slow sharply and peak oil reached by 2030, although this is likely to be followed by a long plateau rather than a sharp drop. We expect global spare capacity to decline as non-OPEC supply growth slows down more rapidly than oil demand growth, limiting the negative impact on prices and keeping long-term marginal cost around $75/bbl. ERM2 = lower CPI target, cautious monetary easing, FX reserves accumulation As part of the move toward ERM2, the inflation target will likely be revised down from 3%, probably to 2.5%, bringing it closer to the ECB’s 2% target. The central bank will also likely become more open to reserve accumulation in preparation for a fixed exchange rate regime, under which the HUF would be pegged to the EUR at a central rate, with a standard fluctuation band of 15%. The recommended range for Foreign Exchange (FX) reserves under such a regime is around EUR70–90bn. Hungary’s official reserves stood at EUR61bn in May and look set to rise to above EUR70bn by year-end, driven mainly by EU fund inflows. Such levels would still be at the lower end of the range. A lower CPI target would require relatively tighter monetary conditions than under a 3% target, but this does not imply tighter conditions relative to today, when ex-post and ex- ante real rates are well above 300bp. Some alternative jobs data have also been stronger. But it is not clear to us whether seasonally elevated employment levels reflect sustained stronger demand for workers or simply some temporary shifts in employment patterns in a series that has become much more volatile. If anything, some more leading indicators like NFIB hiring plans or initial jobless claims suggest some upcoming pullback in payroll employment. And one important reason to take stronger payroll employment with a grain of salt is that the unemployment rate has moved sideways at 4.3%, despite three months of job growth running well above what should be a much lower breakeven rate this year. A stable unemployment rate and subdued wage growth at least suggest that recent data do not reflect a retightening in the labor market. records.text: 12 June 2026 Euro Weekly Digest Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG Week in review ECB rate hike As we anticipated, the European Central Bank raised its key policy rate by 25 basis points to 2.25% at its meeting this week. This was the first hike in a year and, significantly, marks the first such move by a major global central bank in response to the recent energy shock emanating from the Middle East. The decision signals that a 'look through' strategy on energy-driven inflation is not a universally robust policy, and the ECB is opting to now against inevitable indirect inflation pressures. The ECB's communications were carefully balanced, mixing hawkish and dovish elements to keep market expectations anchored amidst high uncertainty. Our AI analysis of the statement and press conference scored the overall tone as slightly more hawkish than in April. Our baseline forecast remains for one more 25bp hike in September, bringing the terminal rate to 2.50% and delivering a measured tightening of policy. This view assumes a US-Iran deal materialises by the end of this month and that euro area GDP growth will be weaker than the ECB's own projections. However, we see risks as tilted to the upside. A terminal rate of 2.75% is more likely than a peak of 2.25%, a risk that could materialise if inflation proves more stubborn or if economic growth is more resilient than expected (for example if the AI cycle results in stronger global growth and sustains the resilience of manufacturing). Looking ahead

records.text: M Idea 2 Reassessing risks to our Fed call after the latest data When we wrote our outlook, we highlighted two scenarios under which inflation would run higher and the Fed would either remain on hold for longer or potentially hike rates: a demand push scenario, and one featuring a persistent oil premium stemming from a prolonged US-Iran conflict. In the demand push scenario, stronger consumption and business investment—supported by elevated wealth and improving confidence—drive a reacceleration in growth and tighter labor market conditions. As a result, inflation pressures remain firm even as oil dynamics normalize, with tighter labor markets reinforcing persistence in core inflation and ultimately prompting the Fed to begin hiking once it becomes clear that the strength reflects demand rather than productivity. By contrast, in the permanent oil premium scenario, oil prices remain structurally elevated, leading to sustained supply side pressures and gradual pass through into core prices. While growth is somewhat softer, inflation remains persistently above target, keeping the Fed cautious and on hold with a high bar for easing. The recent developments in the Middle East, together with last week’s employment report and this week’s inflation data, suggest that both scenarios may be becoming more likely than we initially anticipated. records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 12 June 2026 13 Japan Takayasu Kudo BofAS Japan Izumi Devalier BofAS Japan Pass-through from higher oil prices to CPI to intensify from autumn See complete report: Asia Economic Weekly: Japan: Oil shock: Pipeline pressures set to lift CPI from autumn 12 June 2026 As a net resource importer, Japan faces additional cost-push pressure from higher import prices. Import prices and PPI rebounded in April-May, and the effect should feed into CPI, which has recently been moderating. Based on autoregression (VAR) analysis, a 10% rise in oil prices lifts gasoline prices from the following month. Electricity follows with a lag of about six months. By contrast, ex- energy BoJ core CPI rises more gradually. The impact peaks about one year after the shock and then persists at a similar pace for roughly another year. In the near term, energy CPI will face upward pressure. But government subsidies should sharply limit the rise. Together with negative food base effects, CPI yoy should continue to moderate through the summer. Even so, cost pressures will continue to spread to non-energy items. Broad-based price increases should lift BoJ core CPI. Our estimates suggest a 1.3–1.4ppt boost to Japan- style core CPI in early 2027, implying a move from below 2% to above 3%. records.text: With EU bonds reliably trading in line with Euro area aggregate fundamentals rather than AAA-rated issuers, the hurdle for significant compression of credit premium vs EGB markets is likely to be high. But at the same time, this cheapness vs rating creates a positive valuation for EU bonds and should help limit further spread widening. 2027 and 2028 should see continued market deepening, but with smaller funding needs than in recent years given the end of NGEU issuance. This opens the door for EU bond liquidity to catch-up to peers while mitigating any residual pressures from bond supply. We think risks are thus modestly skewed towards tightening. Further out in time, a key question is whether there will be fresh common borrowing through the EU. The European Commission’s Multi-annual Financial Framework (MFF) proposal entails further support to Ukraine beyond 2027 (and other countries through macro-financial assistance), as well as a new investment program (Catalyst Europe), and a fresh crisis response mechanism. These proposals are currently being debated within the European Parliament and the outcome uncertain. Absent new programmes, a declining free-float would likely undermine EU bond liquidity – although it could of course help bond supply absorption. records.text: 2 Asia Economic Weekly | 12 June 2026 This Week in Focus Amid persistent global volatility, recent data points to mixed economic trends across the region. In China, export continued to remain robust on global tech cycle upswing. CPI inflation steady in May while PPI inflation strength persists. In India, the RBI held the policy rate while flagging risks ahead. The central bank revised its FY27 growth projections lower and inflation higher. In Japan, wage growth remained firm, with broad- based wage growth likely to cushion external headwinds. Meanwhile, in Indonesia, BI turned more proactive with an off-cycle rate hike to stabilize FX and attract capital flows. China: Export growth remained robust; CPI inflation stable, while PPI inflation increased Export growth accelerated to 19.4% yoy in May (vs 15% consensus), up from 14.1% in Apr. Strong demand for tech products remained the key driver, grew at 50.9% yoy (vs 39.5% previously), with IC exports remaining exceptionally robust and ADP equipment exports picking up further. Meanwhile, exports to the US rebounded sharply to 36.2% yoy (from 11.1% in Apr), largely reflecting a low base effect. Import growth also remained elevated at 27.4% yoy in May, following 25.3% in Apr, resulting in a trade surplus of USD105.4bn. In our view, exports are likely to remain supported by the global semiconductor upcycle, despite potential new US tariff risks. Separately, headline CPI inflation remained steady at 1.2% yoy in May. Overall, the CBN’s approach reflects a gradual normalisation strategy, anchoring inflation expectations, rebuilding reserves, and restoring market confidence, while allowing flexibility in both FX and interest rate policy during the transition. On the macro side, higher oil prices and ongoing tax reforms are boosting fiscal revenues. Nigeria’s Debt Management Office (DMO) is implementing a NGN29tn financing plan for the 2026 budget (NGN18tn domestic and NGN10.7tn external). Domestic borrowing is progressing well, with NGN6tn already raised. External borrowing plan amounts to US$7bn. Nigeria has yet to tap markets in 2026, but is diversifying beyond Eurobonds toward concessional lending, export credit agencies (e.g. Italy, United Kingdom (UK), Spain), and syndicated loans. A US$1bn World Bank facility is under negotiation, while a US$5bn 6- year Total Return Swap (TRS) - partly disbursed - adds complexity to the external debt mix. The TRS will be disbursed in three tranches- a first tranche of US$1.5bn already disbursed in May 2026. records.text: 18 Europe Economic Weekly | 12 June 2026 UK: Worsening trade-offs Overall, the tone was cautious on the United Kingdom (UK) in our London Small Talks Symposium. Both monetary and fiscal policy are likely to face big policy trade-offs as the impact from the Iran conflict materializes. Outlook disrupted by the conflict Pre-conflict, the UK economy was reasonably on track for decent growth and gradual return of inflation closer to target. The conflict will likely bring lower growth and higher inflation. Inflationary pressures are likely to intensify from the middle of the year when gas prices rise, and food price pressures materialize. Growth is likely to slow down, but perhaps not as much as feared, with a recession unlikely. The key concern, according to our speakers, is the emergence of slack in the labour market and flattening of real wages. Youth unemployment is a particular issue with weak demand but also supply weighed by ill health. So far, there is conflicting evidence on the risks of second round and indirect effects on inflation from the rise in energy prices. As reported by Bloomberg (1 Jun) the Commerce Secretary has until June 30 to give an updated recommendation to President Donald Trump on tariffs for refined copper — the most widely traded form. Ahead of that decision, the premium of US prices over the rest of the world has expanded again, prompting a renewed flow of metal to American ports. Citi Commodity Strategy believes lingering fears of a potential US tariff on refined copper can support sentiment until July, beyond which inventory draws/reduced incentive to finance metal domestically can act as a headwind. Their base case remains that no tariff will be announced, but that US policymakers may opt to maintain strategic ambiguity rather announcing anything definitive to support continued storage of inventory within the US. This may weigh somewhat through 3Q’26, but our base case of a Hormuz reopening in 3Q’26 may offset downside, and any eventual inventory draws are likely to be gradual rather than sudden. Non-shelter services (supercore) prices were up a modest 0.25%MoM, reflecting a drag from motor vehicle insurance – a category that will likely continue to weigh on CPI in upcoming months. Nigeria: tight policy, strong buffers, and rising borrowings The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) has held policy rates steady at the latest monetary policy committee in May, maintaining a cautious stance amid concerns about second round inflation effects. Inflation reached 15.7% in April from 15.4% in March. Higher fuel and food prices are driving the modest upturn. Compared to peers, food inflation risks are somewhat mitigated by domestic fertiliser production capacity. With policy rate at 26.5% the central bank stance remains restrictive. CBN is likely to remain cautious and stay on hold. CBN could re-evaluate current policy stance should inflation rise close to 20%, though less likely. The balance of payments outlook is improving, reflecting current account surpluses and rising FX reserves. External inflows are strengthening, although official data may understate Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) due to classification issues. The FX market is functioning more smoothly, with improved liquidity and greater tolerance for two-way movements. Fx reserves have strengthened significantly, close to US$50bn and rising organically, supported by higher oil revenues. For this reason, we took off our SPX vs CDX long, halved our Kospi long (for a second time), and slightly trimmed our more strategic equity overweight in GAA last week (but stayed strategically overweight). In the median case, when POLLS triggers, the SPX falls by ~2% within the 1m aftermath. If the signal triggers only briefly, as it did this time, the decline extends to a more significant 3-4% in the next 30-50 trading days. At the lows, we were down by around 4.5%, triggering some questions about when to re-enter the market. Let’s first answer this from a technical / back-testing perspective. On this point, we would note that our existing POLLS backtest keeps us out of the market for a month (re-enter the market after POLLS stays consistently below 18 for 22 trading days), suggesting re-entry in late June. Alternatively, we noted in the past that a very low POLLS reading is also a good buying signal. We test this in Figure 2 and find that a level of 9 or lower is required to trigger a re-entry that outperforms the unconditional and significantly outperforms the 1m rule. On redundancies, our suite of models still point to a similar 125-150k range in the three months to April. And on vacancies, high frequency trackers suggest a steeper drop to 690k. Inflation: After a bigger-than-expected drop in inflation over April, we expect a little more of a bounce in the data. Indeed, some of the drop in services prices will likely unwind into May. Food and core goods prices will also likely see some lingering price pressures. Positive base effects will also push up on headline inflation. Where do we see May inflation landing? We see headline CPI inching higher to 3.01% y-o-y, with core CPI stepping up to 2.72% y-o-y. Services CPI, we estimate, will jump to 3.65% y-o-y. And RPI, we think, will run up to 3.33% y-o-y. Looking ahead, the inflation trajectory points to further upside. We expect more price pressures to build in the coming months – particularly as dual-fuel bills reset in July. The ongoing energy shock is keeping price momentum elevated for longer too. The longer the shock lasts, the more likely we see a further ratchet higher of indirect effects (namely, via food and core goods). We expect CPI to track around 3.1% y-o-y this year, before slowing to 2.6% y-o-y next year. See our full preview here. Retail Sales: Some bounce back in retail spending looks likely. That said, we suspect the interpretation of this data might differ across the MPC. What next? We see binary scenarios ahead. One where the supply of commodities out of the Middle East starts to normalise in the coming weeks would mean very little chance of policy tightening this year, we think. In a scenario where disruptions in the supply of oil and gas persist for months, and commodity prices readjust higher, we think hikes become likely - we think 2 hikes look probable in this scenario, with July a very live meeting. Our modal case remains a hold throughout 2026. Rates Strategy: We maintain a medium-term bullish view on the front end, but see mildly hawkish risks into next week's MPC meeting as it remains uncertain whether the Committee will receive the benign geopolitical resolution it may have hoped for in April. Market focus will likely be on the policy messaging, individuals' respective paragraphs and the vote split. From a valuation perspective, markets have already priced in considerable optimism that a geopolitical agreement can be reached relatively soon. This leaves front-end rates vulnerable to a repricing higher should these expectations be disappointed.

As during past interventions, this time as well the value of securities holdings fell by around the same amount. records.text: United States: Money Markets SOFR/FF: Going long July We have been calling for continued softness in funding markets, and see value in going long July SOFR/FF. The TGA is set to be lower for much of July, keeping funding soft even as it peaks late in the month. Bill issuance is hefty, but the effect on SOFR should be less than feared. This is a reprint of United States Money Markets: OFR/FF: Going long July, published on June 11, 2026. We continue to expect very smooth funding conditions in the months ahead (see here), and see value in expressing that view in SOFR/FF space. As we have highlighted previously, funding pressures may begin to pick up in late July as the Treasury ramps up bill issuance and the TGA balance rises toward $1trn, draining reserves from the banking system (see here). Fears over this build have kept July SOFR/FF levels negative, but the TGA level is likely to be quite low through much of July, given large payment needs early in the month and the methodical pace of cash build from bill issuance. This should leave funding conditions relatively soft for most of July, with any pressures concentrated later in the month. Growing bank intermediation capacity should also help. In fact, we estimate that average reserve levels in July will be slightly higher than in June. We think supply concerns have kept July SOFR/FF tighter than fair value. The drag is largely cyclical and front loaded: tariff effects weighed on real purchasing power in 1Q, while the subsequent oil disruption is acting as an effective tax on households through 2Q and 3Q. In that environment, growth has rotated away from consumption toward other components, even as underlying demand has remained broadly intact. Taking stock of incoming data, the pace of spending is tracking close to expectations. Real consumption growth had slowed to 1.4% q/q saar in 1Q26. Beneath the surface, the drivers of spending have improved modestly. Recent labor market gains imply that the nominal payroll proxy for production and non-supervisory workers is running a solid pace: 5.5% in April and May over the 1Q average (2m/3m % saar), and 4.4% for all employees. However, headline PCE growth in 2Q will continue to pressure real labor market income; a further acceleration in the labor market this summer could lead to real wage growth closer to flat, rather than slightly negative, and could incrementally support near-term consumption momentum. In countries where internet retailing is a small share of transactions, retailers tend to tie their online prices to offline prices in order to minimise costs associated with making pricing decisions. In countries where online transactions have a significant market share, online and offline prices are closely related and online prices may lead offline as the demographic of computer-literate, middle-class, cash-rich and time-poor consumers to which online retailers sell are less price-sensitive than the average consumer. As purchasing habits change, these online price series capture prices and changes in product information and can provide real time information on consumer behaviour. Executing on this sale should open the door to a fast de-leveraging of the group and a healthy total yield for investors on a 12m view. We see 2026 guidance as conservative and believe organic growth should improve from 1Q26 as price-hikes come through, UHP mix accelerates and US/EU truck cycles gradually recover. Key Debates / Pushback – The degree to which higher pricing/raw mats may drive further consumer trade-down and the degree to which at higher rates ContiTech valuations could be lowered or a sale delayed. Valuation – Stock remains cheap on a total yield basis with ContiTech proceeds we think allowing for a 12%+ total yield over the next 12m. Shares trade 10x P/E with a ~8% FCFY based on o a high and growing FCF margin. Risks – Key risks are further consumer trade-down, continues raw mat inflation and any delayed US truck cycle recovery. Outside of this any sustain economic weakness in DM could drive down miles driven/truck activity from even these low levels and could limit organic growth over the next 2 years. records.text: Bear Market Checklist Our Bear Market Checklist (BMC) is not intended to be a market-timing tool. Instead, it advises on what to do when the inevitable dips come along. It does that by measuring how excessive the previous peak was. The frothier the market high, the less inclined the BMC is to suggest buying into the ensuing dip. Our global BMC has now at 10/18 red flags, driven primarily by valuations. We also see exuberance building in sentiment, Capex Growth, and RoE. The BMC looks benign in Europe (just 5/18 red flags). The US looks frothier at 11.5/18. Source: Citi Research, DataStream, MSCI, FactSet, Dealogic, Lipper 14 Prepared for Cayla Buettner

To get a sense, we constructed a meeting-by-meeting measure of ECB sentiment. It is based on the monetary policy statements (MPS), and we use AI to identify sentences referring to already observed activity. The classifier deliberately excludes projections, risks and policy-rate guidance. To reduce model-run noise, we average the score across repeated classification runs. Let's be clear, this is a quick and simplistic exercise, and we don’t pretend to have the perfect measure of ECB sentiment. Still, the index we construct shows an interesting pattern. records.text: 12 June 2026 UK economic notes Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG How has the economy changed since the April MPR? The April MPR came with no central projections, with the MPC opting for three scenarios instead: n In Scenario A, oil and gas prices followed the paths implied by futures curves. The combination of the relatively short-lived energy shock and weakness in demand was assumed to be enough to prevent any second- round effects in response to the shock. n In Scenario B, energy prices peaked at similar levels but remained higher over the rest of the forecast than in Scenario A. Second-round effects were assumed to be modest. n In Scenario C, energy prices rose sharply and remained elevated for a prolonged period. The larger energy shock was assumed to lead to much stronger second-round effects than in Scenario B. The economy - at least on the surface - has been stronger than the Bank assumed. GDP growth, to start the year, was stronger than the Bank anticipated. But the labour market has softened a touch, relative to the Bank's expectations. And in good news for the MPC, price pressures have eased by a little more than expected. In short, despite a hotter start to GDP, the cooling labour market and better price data may just about buy the MPC a little more time in assessing its next course of action. Indeed, back in early March, the macro consensus was that the longer the closure persisted, the more severe the impact on growth and inflation could be. However, this assumed a linear relationship between the duration of the conflict and oil and gas prices. Given the drawdown in the US reserves, as well as the drop in China imports, oil prices are now decently sub-USD100/ bbl. records.text: 11 June 2026 Focus Europe Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG Hawkish elements Not an insurance hike President Lagarde strongly pushed back at the description of this as an “insurance” hike. This is not a preemptive tightening against an inherently uncertain event. The ECB sees this hike as robust across all the scenarios under consideration, including the new milder (sub-baseline) scenario. The hike is justifiable on the basis of what the ECB already knows about the inflation shock. This is consistent with what we argued about the risk of persistent inflation in our Preview. Core HICP revised up Relative to our expectations, the biggest surprise in the staff macro projections was the upward revision to the core HICP forecasts. Core is seen at 2.5% in both 2026 and 2027 and 2.2% in 2028. These are 0.1pp, 0.2pp and 0.1pp above what we expected. These upward revisions to core inflation reflect the indirect and second round effects that the ECB anticipates. Lagarde said the ECB is already beginning to see a “broadening” of inflation, meaning indirect effects, and expects indirect effects in food, goods and services prices. Even in the final quarter of 2028, the end of the forecast trajectory, core HICP is above target at 2.2% - and this is under the conditioning assumption of three rate hikes, up from two in March. records.text: 11 June 2026 UK economic notes Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 What do survey data tell us? The latest BRC Shop Price data highlighted continued weakness in clothing prices (0.2% m-o-m) but a big jump in furniture prices (2% m-o-m). Electrical goods prices were up 1.5% m-o-m. DIY/Gardening goods saw prices up 1.5% m-o-m. And books/stationary prices edged up by 0.2% m-o-m. Health and beauty items were up 0.2% m-o-m in May. All in all, we expect monthly inflation to push higher in May. Our own models point to a rebound in health goods prices (0.4% m-o-m, CPI). We see 'other non-durables' prices up 0.2% m-o-m (CPI). Across semi-durables, we see clothing (including textiles) inflation pushing up by 0.8% m-o-m (CPI). And on durables, we see furniture prices up 1.3% m-o-m (CPI). On cars, Auto-Trader's Used Car Index saw a meaningful rise on like-for-like prices (up to 0.7% y-o-y). We pencil in a 0.8% m-o-m rise (CPI). On IT goods, we expect a 0.8% m-o-m drop. Where does this leave our projections for core goods? For CPI, we see core goods prices up 0.54% m-o-m, taking the annual rate slightly down to 1.04%. For RPI, we see the core goods (NEIG) basket up 0.44% m-o-m, pulling the annual rate down to 2.17%. records.text: The Path Ahead Looking ahead, we continue to expect output growth to run below trend through the rest of 2026. Higher energy prices should weigh on real disposable income and consumer spending, while tighter financial conditions should also slow momentum. Weaker growth should result in further labour market softening, with the unemployment rate likely to rise to 5.4% in the second half of the year. We expect inflation to rise notably in the second half of the year, peaking at 3.7% in Q4. Energy prices are likely to rise further in July on the back of an increase in the Ofgem price cap, while the indirect effects of the energy shock should result in an increase in food inflation. Increasing supply chain pressures suggest that core goods inflation is also likely to rise. That said, we continue to expect that the weaker cyclical backdrop will limit the extent of second-round effects. As such, we expect inflation to decelerate notably in 2027. There remain substantial risks around our growth and inflation estimates given ongoing uncertainties around the outlook for energy prices. But if our baseline projections are realised then we think that the MPC is most likely to remain on hold throughout 2026 (before lowering Bank Rate in 2027) given an already restrictive policy stance, tighter financial conditions, and the loosening labour market. Q3: How will the measure relating to external commercial borrowings generate flows? The RBI’s USD–rupee FX swap facility for external commercial borrowings with an average maturity of three years or more will be applicable to borrowings drawn after the date of the circular until 31 December 2026. This facility is available to corporates with majority state ownership (known as PSUs) and Authorized Dealer Category-I banks that raise overseas foreign currency borrowings with a minimum maturity of three years. The facility allows PSUs and authorized banks to borrow dollars and convert them into INR with hedge costs subsidized by the RBI. That lowers the effective borrowing rate to below that of domestic borrowing. We think this incentive will encourage these companies to tap into this facility before the end of the year. India raised about USD45bn through such borrowing last year. As the facility is limited to PSUs and authorized banks but providing substantial savings for them, we estimate the inflows generated may be around USD15– 20bn. In recent quarters, ROE for the aggregate S&P 500 has benefited from the growing weight of the mega-cap tech stocks while ROE for the median S&P 500 company has declined. The seven largest tech stocks currently have a collective ROE of 44%, which has expanded by 900 bp during the past three years. The AI capex boom has lifted semiconductor profitability but will be an n increasing headwind to mega-cap tech ROE going forward. The hyperscalers have grown in asset intensity and experienced declining sales/asset turnover since the start of the AI boom. During the next few years, rising hyperscaler depreciation expenses will reverse some of the S&P 500 ROE benefit that AI capex has generated in the form of elevated semiconductor profit margins. Equity raises to fund investment spending will also pressure ROE. Consensus estimates imply that ROE for the seven largest technology stocks will decline by an average of 700 bp next year. AI also creates a key long-term upside case for ROE, both for the mega-cap n tech stocks and for the broad equity market. Chair Warsh has noted that "The Fed’s bloated balance sheet, designed to support the biggest firms in a bygone crisis era, can be reduced significantly. That largesse can be redeployed in the form of lower interest rates to support households and small and medium-size businesses. " The interaction between the policy rate and the balance sheet is not discussed much in the market. Chair Warsh potentially could argue that a tightening of financial conditions— if warranted— could be achieved by reducing the balance sheet, rather than by significantly raising the policy rate. Such an argument would be perceived as reducing the right tail of hikes but increasing term premium at the long end. Still, any changes in balance sheet policy are likely to be put in place with much deliberation and not soon. Where does that leave us? Putting all the above together, we believe the FOMC outcome will be neutral, as Chair Warsh would want his first outing to not rock the boat, to a touch dovish versus market pricing. Because BoJ core CPI excludes energy, this suggests that higher import prices are being passed through to some extent from upstream to downstream corporate sectors and ultimately to consumers. BoJ core CPI inflation, which is not directly affected by government energy subsidies, is currently continuing to slow, reflecting the flip-side of the sharp rise in food prices during 2025 ( Figure 19). This y/y base effect looks likely to continue exerting relatively strong downward pressure through at least summer. However, the impact of import prices, which have already started rising due to higher crude oil prices and JPY weakness, should gradually outweigh the food-related y/y base effect, with BoJ core CPI inflation likely to turn higher again. We expect it to peak at around 2.5% in spring 2027, then stabilize at around 2% from summer onward. At the June meeting, the BoJ will conduct an interim assessment of its QT program, under which it has been gradually reducing JGB purchases. This time around, the focus will be on the direction of reductions from April 2027 onward. In his 3 June speech, Governor Ueda did not go into specific policy details. However, he positively assessed the fact that, partly as a result of QT , the JGB market is gradually regaining the functions originally expected of it, while also emphasizing the need to keep a close watch on JGB market stability. Indeed, the BoJ’s diffusion index (DI) of bond market functioning has improved considerably, even though it remains below the level seen before the introduction of yield curve control (YCC; Figure 6). Meanwhile, long- term yields remain on an upward trend, having exceeded the levels seen before QQE under Governor Kuroda ( Figure 7). Recently, concerns over fiscal expansion by the Takaichi administration appear to have been a major factor pushing up long-term yields, but the situation seems to be approaching a point where the BoJ cannot ignore it either. In light of this speech, we came to assume that from FY27 onward, the BoJ would either keep monthly purchases at around JPY2trn, a level that would be reached as planned in March 2027, or slow the pace of reduction. If all corporates act in a similar manner, there is no market share loss for individual firms. If these indirect effects are sufficiently large, they can raise headline inflation in such a way that risks of second-round effects would rise too. Beyond September, risk premia for some further policy tightening are likely to persist given that indirect and second round risks will linger. But, if we are right about the scale of these effects – curbed by slow growth – the ECB probably won’t need to hike more than twice in total. records.text: US Economics Weekly12 June 2026 ab 9 Big game, limited impact: world cuponomics The 2026 world cup — co-hosted by the United States, Canada and Mexico — kicked off this week and clients have asked about the potential impact on the US economy. Sporting events of this scale can generate substantial short-term economic activity through increased tourism, consumer spending, and infrastructure investment. Historically, host countries anticipate large inflows of visitors and related spending, contributing to higher demand in hospitality, transportation, and retail sectors. The expansion to 48 teams in 2026 may further amplify these effects by increasing the number and geographic spread of matches. It is also worth noting that the US will host 78 of the 104 matches and all of the games from the quarter-finals onward. That said, based on historical evidence and the incoming data, we expect relatively little impact on headline GDP , inflation, or labor market figures. FIFA estimates a $17.1 billion impact on US GDP as a result of the tournament, which is 0.05% of GDP in a ~$31 trillion economy. Limited shock, limited momentum for “More Europe” While disruptions related to the Iran conflict and evolving energy dynamics are significant, they are smaller in magnitude than the 2022 shock. As a result, the sense of urgency across the EU is weaker, and this means limited fiscal response and marginal use of flexibility within the EU fiscal framework. Last week’s decision by the EU to allow countries to reallocate 0.3% of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of their defence-clause related energy measures was not seen a gamechanger for those EU countries that haven’t activated the defence escape clause yet. Recall that 15 EU countries activated the National Escape Clause (NEC) in 2025, and Spain requested it this Spring. (see Europe Economic Weekly: Relentless vs reluctant ). At the same time, there has been no meaningful lowering of the threshold for advancing “More Europe” initiatives, whether in energy policy, defence strategy or broader integration efforts. In essence, smaller shocks are resulting in more muted policy ambition. Sources: Company disclosures, BNP Paribas Fig. 1: Japanese city banks’ deposit–lending gap (JPYtrn) Banks’ loan-deposit gap shrinks and duration-risk tolerance falls: While loan growth remains solid at city banks, deposits are either lagging or even falling in some cases, narrowing the loan-deposit gap. The gap has historically been considered as a source of funding for banks to purchase JGB. During the long deflationary period, the gap kept widening, giving the impression that Japanese banks had an unlimited buying power. However, after the ‘unconventional easing’ policy, much of the banks’ JGB holdings were replaced by the Bank of Japan’s reserves, allowing them to tap those balances to buy bonds for a while. If the loan-deposit gap continues to shrink while the BoJ’s balance-sheet reduction drains overall reserve balances, the banks’ capacity to purchase JGB would diminish, in our view. Even now, an asset-liability management officer who believes that the gap will be filled over time by loan growth is less likely to lock funds into long-dated bonds. For China, policy continues to guide gradual appreciation, reinforced by structural anchors: a persistent current account surplus and ongoing exporter repatriation. External balances remain supportive overall, with improving FX settlement and steady capital flows reinforcing the yuan’s relative resilience, bolstered by a valuation discount (Figure 3 and here). In contrast, INR pressures remain persistent. India recorded roughly USD5bn equity outflows in May, followed by an additional ~USD3.5bn of outflows in just the first week of June, underscoring a continued foreign exodus (Figure 3). records.text: M Idea 2 Inflation Linked Bonds United States | Identifying Rich/Cheap Bonds MORGAN STANLEY & CO. LLC Aryaman Singh Aryaman@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-1993 Matthew Hornbach, CMT Matthew.Hornbach@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-1863 Martin Tobias, CFA, CMT Martin.Tobias@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-6076 Shaun Zhou Shaun.Zhou@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-3348 Eli Carter Eli.Carter@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-4703 Bond yields are driven by macro factors such as inflation data, Fed expectations, growth concerns, or shifts in risk sentiment. They are also driven by shorter-term demand and supply dynamics. These forces can affect the entire yield curve, a specific sector of the curve, or an individual bond. In order to identify which bonds are trading rich or cheap in a bond universe, we price each bond based on the curve implied yield. To price the cash flows of each bond, we need the spot curve or zero curve. In Treasuries, we have more than 340 bonds which give us a rich set of observations across maturities, making it easier to estimate spot curve, par curve, and get model implied yield of a bond. In TIPS, the universe is smaller, especially in the front end, which makes curve construction a bit challenging. In this piece, we walk through the framework for calculating spot, par yields and identify rich and cheap bonds in nominal Treasuries and TIPS. On the turn itself, our observation is that EURCZK xccy has consistently tightened into year end in recent years. We attribute this to the tendency for year-end EUR liquidity premia to be priced in with a negative skew earlier in the calendar and subsequently compress as market participants gain clearer visibility on EUR funding needs into December. China also retains ~900-k b/d of crude oil import capacity via pipelines from Russia and Central Asia, forming the backbone of its overland crude oil supply system, with crude oil shipments via rail providing marginal flexibility. The ESPO Skovorodino–Daqing spur alone accounts for the bulk of Russia–China flows at ~675-kb/d, while the Kazakhstan–China system contributes ~240-k b/d via the Atasu–Alashankou link, effectively functioning as an oil swap route where Russian crude is delivered into Kazakhstan and re-exported into China. Rail flows remain marginal but flexible, with shipments via Mongolia typically capped at ~ 30-kb/d, acting as a minor balancing mechanism rather than a structural route. In addition, Russia has explored incremental crude-by-rail capacity through East Siberian hubs such as the Meget rail tank loading station (60–145-k b/d), which is currently not operational but under discussion for restart, reinforcing its role as minor swing capacity rather than a steady supply source. Based on preliminary data/estimates from OilX, China’s refinery runs fell sharply to near 13-m b/d in May’26 from ~15.4-m b/d in Feb’26, yet product balances proved more resilient than the crude throughput decline would suggest.
