records.text: ab 11 June 2026 Global Research European Economic Comment ECB: Sticking to our call of a pause in July Key conclusions from the ECB press conference As firmly expected, the ECB hiked the depo rate by 25bps to 2.25% today. We drew the following key conclusions from the press conference: First, the decision to hike rates was unanimous and seen by the Governing Council as comprehensively justified by the ECB new macro baseline forecast as well as the three alternative scenarios. Second, we cannot conclude that today's hike was a "one and done", we think at least one more hike will follow. Third, we cannot conclude that the next hike will definitely come already in the meeting on 23 July (although we cannot rule it out either). Fourth, as regards the question whether the ECB will deliver another 25bps or 50bps of rate hikes - the market is currently pricing another 42.7bps until year-end - we did not receive firm signals today. We expect only one more hike, in September Our own baseline forecast remains that the ECB will pause at the July meeting, but then hike rates by another 25bps to 2.5% in September. However, we will follow data carefully ahead of the July meeting, particularly with regards to data that might change the ECB's assessment on the emergence of pro-inflationary second round effects - see our heatmap in Figure 3. Through the end of the year, we expect employment (in both surveys) will have averaged slightly below a monthly breakeven rate of ~ 30k/month, and the unemployment rate will be around 4.6-4.7%. 2) Falling participation of older workers Changes in labor force participation – due to either demographic changes or other labor market conditions – remain a significant source of uncertainty for the unemployment rate this year. Since April 2025 (the highest level in the last year), the labor force participation rate has declined by 0.8pp to 61.8%. Of course, an unemployment rate stable around 4.3% while participation and labor force growth have slowed substantially implicitly suggests demand has weakened in line with supply. Figure 20. records.text: 2 Insights SPOTLIGHT VIEWS: WHAT’S DRIVING FX? In a world where central banks don’t matter? This week marks the start of the next round of G10 central bank meetings. Most are expected to remain on hold, except for the ECB and BoJ, where hikes are priced. While we continue to monitor developments closely, it is increasingly clear that policy expectations are having less influence on spot markets, despite a bifurcated backdrop of some central banks holding and others tightening. The 15-day correlation between real money DM FX flows and 1-year forward rate expectations is now close to zero (Figure 3). One explanation is that front-end rate volatility has meaningfully subsided—while not quite back to pre-war levels, it is approaching them. This suggests that, despite ongoing geopolitical risks and an evolving data backdrop, markets are broadly comfortable with current pricing over the next 12 months. For FX, the key question is what could disrupt this dynamic. Given that the correlation tends to re-emerge when pricing adjusts more sharply, it would likely take a meaningful geopolitical or data surprise capable of prompting a central bank reaction. We saw elements of this on Friday, when a stronger-than-expected US labor print led markets to more firmly price in a Fed hike, reinforcing tactical USD strength. Second, the starting point for the Euro area economy is different, with ECB rate policy at neutral and ECB balance sheet policy already tightening. Third, recent improvement in Southern European fundamentals (see here and here), combined with various policies designed to backstop spreads (NGEU, TPI), all point to the resilience of sovereign credit. records.text: Record profitability has been one of the factors supporting high S&P 500 valuations. The current S&P 500 trailing 4-quarter return on equity (“ROE”) is 22%, the highest on record. Although the P/E is elevated relative to history, it is roughly in line with the fair value indicated by our macro models. Just as investors typically assign higher valuation multiples to stocks with higher profitability, history suggests that the profitability of the aggregate equity market helps determine its P/E multiple, along with macro factors like interest rates and inflation. Variation in profitability also helps explain the variation in valuations across equity indices. The relationship between ROE and P/E valuation multiples is evident both among US equity indices and across a selection of major global indices. records.text: European Rates Weekly 12 June 2026 Citi Research 17 Risks of an increase in EIB’s funding total target are low. EIB sets its next year’s funding target around December every year, and the total borrowing authorization also includes €5bn for prefinancing the following year’s funding needs. This is also the case for 2026, and we measure the total issuance progress against the total borrowing authorization, i.e., we include the possible prefinancing amount. As such, EIB’s funding plan already includes flexibility to prefinance next year’s maturities without increasing the funding target, and we believe it is likely, despite the strong issuance progress, that the 2026 funding target remains unchanged. Increased longer-dated supply by EIB also appears unlikely. The overall weighted-average maturity (WAM) of EIB’s benchmark supply in the main funding currency has been around 7 years for the past 15 years. It increased significantly for the EUR supply during the ECB QE, which also pushed up the aggregate WAM across the main funding currencies, but since 2021 it has steadily declined and converged with the WAM of its USD supply which tends to be shorter-dated. This contrasts with EU’s WAM that is significantly higher at 11.8y YTD (Figure 28). Moreover, EIB has already issued €11bn YTD in 10y+ (43% of its € benchmark supply, of which €5bn this month), which is broadly in line with the 2020–25 average (€12bn; Figure 29). The ECB hiked 25bp to 2.25%. This is the first change in ECB policy rates for a year, the first hike by the ECB since September 2023 and – importantly – the first hike by one of the major global central banks in response to the Middle East energy shock. This is significant. It means the ‘look through’ strategy is not a robust policy response, at least not in every region. This decision is not without debate, of course. There was a certain degree of balance within the ECB communications, with some slightly more hawkish elements counterbalanced by slightly more dovish elements, helping to keep market pricing anchored around three hikes. In the context of still elevated uncertainty – about the situation in the Middle East, about the path of energy prices and about the propagation of energy inflation into general inflation – it is understandable why the ECB does not want to send significant signals. Our baseline is unchanged. We look for one more hike to 2.50% in September. Our baseline assumes a US-Iran deal by the end of June and weaker GDP growth than the ECB expects. Investor Behavior: Rate Hikes May Also Weigh on Duration Demand In this section, we review investor behavior during rate hike cycles. It is often argued that when rate hikes proceed gradually, behind-the-curve dynamics lead to steepening pressure, whereas if the pace of rate hikes accelerates, expectations for long-term yields become more anchored, leading to flattening pressure. However, it should also be noted that rate hikes and rising yields can, in some cases, lead many investors to scale back their investments in JPY-denominated bonds. Below, we summarize investor behavior by type, and we would highlight that demand for JPY bonds from some overseas investors, banks, and life insurers is likely to remain subdued. Regardless of whether rate hikes are implemented, it appears difficult to expect a dramatic improvement in JGB supply-demand conditions unless the macro environment shifts toward one characterized by increasing downside risks to growth and a pause in rate hikes. While such a scenario cannot be ruled out, it is not considered the base case at present. Of course, establishment and household employment may also diverge due to conceptual differences in addition to measurement issues. Household employment is a broader measure of total employment. Since January (when household estimates will reflect the latest population update), weakness in household employment has been partly due to self-employed workers, which would not be reflected in payrolls. Wage and salary employment is the subset of household employment most conceptually similar to payroll employment. This remained strong in March. It has only been over April and May that wage and salary household employment is clearly weaker than payrolls. Two months of divergence is not so abnormal. Payroll employment also reflects the number of jobs, with individual workers only counted as employed once in the household survey, even if they hold multiple jobs. The number of people holding multiple jobs has moved sideways, suggesting this does not explain stronger payroll employment compared to household employment. records.text: 12 June 2026 UK economic notes Page 4 Deutsche Bank AG contracted by 0.1% m-o-m, with consumers registering the biggest pullback in spending. Survey data have pointed to a drop off in momentum. The latest PMI data showed the composite output index dipping into contraction territory, with falls led by both the services and construction sectors. Retail spending looks tepid too - though the summer heat wave in May could temporarily lift spending. Housing activity looks set to drop off on the back of higher rates – as per the latest RICS report. And business investment seems poised to reverse course as business confidence wanes. To be sure, a weakening labour market will also continue to impact spending. The energy shock in and of itself will squeeze real disposable incomes, increasing both the cost of living and cost of doing business. Relative to the MPC’s scenarios, we see GDP growth tracking closer to Scenario A, with output a little more resilient on the back of stronger catch up in Q1-26. Q2-26 GDP growth looks poised to push closer to 0.1-0.2% q-o-q. And annual GDP growth this year looks set to beat the BoE staff projection of 0.9%, with growth likely to push upwards of 1%. records.text: overall balance sheet of the consumer continues to be healthy, there could be some headwinds. Nominal household wealth gains slowed in 1Q26 with implications for how much upside risk there could be for consumption going forward. Our wealth model indicates that consumption has been running above levels implied by household wealth for the last year, suggesting some upside risk to the saving rate and, correspondingly, downside risk to spending. So, while income dynamics are likely stabilizing, the upside risk to consumption growth from wealth effects is much less likely. Our view then is that real consumption growth is so far evolving largely in line with our baseline: a slower pace of growth most of this year, with some acceleration in 4Q26 onwards, but not a primary driver of growth. Risks around this profile remain skewed slightly to the downside if cyclical factors turn less favorable due to an extended oil disruption, particularly from slower income growth or asset market volatility. Absent a more durable acceleration in labor market momentum and “animal spirits,” we see limited scope for a material upside surprise to consumer spending from here.

Higher prices could weigh on demand if sustained, although the impact is likely to differ across regions and sectors, depending on a range of factors including storage buffers, subsidies, and end-user affordability. We believe that oil consumption tends to show limited sensitivity to short-term price volatility; substantial adjustments are anticipated only if prices rise markedly (e.g., close to $150/bbl) and remain over time. Even in 2022, when the average price was $99/bbl, oil demand rose by 3Mb/d. Although some of this growth could be attributed to the post-Covid rebound, overall, we believe it demonstrates the resilience of demand. Therefore, the most direct effect for now is likely to come through disruptions from shortages of products like LPG and jet fuel. To date, we have observed a pace of demand destruction faster than expected. We now model 2Q demand down 3.0Mb/d w/w, compared to our previous estimate of 2.6Mb/d, primarily due to extended disruptions at Hormuz. Within this, LPG sees a notable decrease of 0.3Mb/d, followed by reductions in motor gasoline and gasoil, each down 0.2 Mb/d. Elevated gasoline prices and low inventories would lower driving activity during the summer, particularly in the US. Let's start with a bit of data work and try to explain why we think EA growth will be 0.3%Y in 2026, while the ECB just published 0.8%Y. And why this is not a fundamental disagreement about the pace ahead. There are two key factors behind this 50bp gap. First, the ECB projections were finalized on 27 May and do not have on board Eurostat´s update released on 5 June, with EA 2Q26 growth now estimated at - 0.2%Q instead of 0.15%Q. As we discussed earlier this week (here), this negative print reflects a sharp drop of GDP in Ireland after exports normalized at the start of the year. From a pure accounting perspective, a revised 1Q26 explains already 35bp (ie 70%!) of the difference between our forecast and the ECB. Second, we also differ with the ECB regarding the expected contribution of Ireland to EA GDP growth in the upcoming quarters. The ECB assumes it will add ca 10bp to EA quarterly growth in 2Q26, 3Q26 and 4Q26. Since Ireland weighs 4% of the EA, this means that Ireland grows by ca 2.5%Q in each of these quarters. Now Ireland GDP numbers are notoriously volatile, so it is hard to have a strong view here. But our reading of the first quarter of 2026 is that this was a normalization after the sizeable export frontloading of 2025. records.text: EEMEA Outlook Holding for now; cuts and hikes ahead We expect the CNB to remain on hold next week despite hawkish comments from MPC members and see room for 300bp of cuts in H2 27. Yet, disinflation in Egypt is likely transitory while rising South Africa CPI raises the prospects of further SARB tightening. Turkiye: Inflation, rates, C/A deficit and reserves all depend on energy prices The CBT kept the policy rate unchanged at 37%, in line with both our and consensus expectations. There were no material changes in the statement. The CBT noted some improvement in the underlying trend of inflation in May, while also highlighting that the slowdown in economic activity has continued into Q2 26. Looking ahead, we expect monthly CPI to stabilise at ~2% m/m (SA) through Q3 26, easing to ~1.5% m/m in Q4 26 – implying an annual print of 29.1% y/y by YE26. Assuming Brent moderates to $90/bbl on average in H2 26, we expect the CBT to lower the average funding rate from 40% to 37% from July, and to cut the policy rate by 100bp at each of the final three MPC meetings (10 September, 22 October, 10 December), bringing it to 34% by YE26. Risks are skewed to the upside, mainly around the energy price outlook ( Turkiye CBT Review: Steady for now, easing ahead, 11 June). In Jan–Apr, the C/A deficit reached $29.4bn, widening by $6.8bn y/y. Of this deterioration, core goods accounted for $5.9bn, while the services surplus declined by $0.7bn. records.text: We Expect a 7-2 Vote for a Hold and Unchanged Guidance Given this backdrop, the Committee looks very likely to hold Bank Rate at 3.75% at next week’s (June 18) meeting. We expect a 7-2 vote, with Pill and Greene likely to dissent in favour of a 25bp hike given their recent comments. In our baseline, Mann votes with the majority for a hold given her focus on financial conditions, but it is very possible that she could join the dissenters given her past voting pattern. Given that the latest comments from Bailey have had a similar tone to the communications at the April meeting, we expect the guidance language to be largely unchanged. The Committee is likely to indicate that a hold is appropriate at this meeting but reiterate that it will continue to monitor the situation in the Middle East closely and that it “stands ready to act as necessary” to contain inflationary pressures. We expect Bailey to emphasise in his individual paragraph that a hold is justified given weakness in the real economy. But we think that he will refrain from giving a strong steer on the path ahead given uncertainty around the magnitude of second-round effects. The risks around our baseline for the communications are probably skewed in a hawkish direction, with some chance that the Summary indicates that risks of second-round effects have continued to build. We detail our thoughts below: HY Cyclicals: Negative On paper, Cyclicals look respectable, with a slight positive expected return in our base case (Figure 13) of tight and unchanged spreads, and only limited negative expected return in a downside scenario of spread widening, and mid-range valuations (Figure 14). framework. The existing stock of non-resident debt is only around US$400mn, which is unlikely to pose systemic outflow risks. Budget optics better than details, positive near-term financing trends, EUR bias The fiscal position is more nuanced than the headline numbers suggest. The headline deficit will be revised down, but for technical reasons – namely, the reclassification of external support as revenue rather than debt financing – rather than due to any genuine improvement in the public finances. In the near term, Ukraine is set to receive unusually large disbursements, with more than US$10bn expected in June alone, mostly from various EU financing facilities. With the debt composition shifting decisively toward EUR, the authorities are fundamentally rethinking their funding currency strategy. USD-denominated debt now accounts for less than 20% of the debt stock, while the central bank still holds more than 60% of its reserves in USD. Over time, that balance will need to adjust, as per authorities.

records.text: Q2 activity contracts, set for weak growth in Q2 Monthly GDP contracted 0.1% m/m in April, having grown 0.3% m/m in March. The contraction was in line with our expectation for services, at -0.2% m/m, and for industrial production, at 0.0% m/m, but a little stronger in construction, at 0.1% m/m, which tipped the headline number at the rounding. It does not, however, change our tracking of Q2 GDP growth at 0.1% q/q. For more see First Look: April GDP, 12 June. BoE surveys show evidence of second-round effects... Two Bank of England surveys this week highlighted one of the main risks to our inflation outlook — that rising inflation expectations lead to greater second-round effects. Household inflation expectations in the BoE/Ipsos quarterly survey increased in Q2 at the one year, the 1y1y and the five-year ahead horizons. The move was more pronounced in the shorter-term measures, with the medium-term measures rising 30bp and 20bp, respectively, from Q1, to 3.5% and 3.9%. There was also an increase in the dispersion of inflation expectations, with the tails of the distribution widening ( Figure 1) . These series are at elevated levels (the five-year measure is the highest it has been since the series began in 2009) and we think will give some concern to the MPC, but we note that the survey was in the field 30 April to 5 May. records.text: US Economics Weekly12 June 2026 ab 10 While the authors did not identify a precise estimate of the event's economic impact on South Korea and Japan, they found only a 0.8% probability that the 2002 world cup generated $4 billion or more — the amount spent on stadiums— and a 93.7% probability that the impact was negative. Data showed limited net tourism gains and clear substitution effects: increases in some visitors (like European tourists to South Korea) were offset by declines in others (like Japanese tourists), leaving total foreign arrivals largely unchanged. Some sectors benefited (such as consumer goods like televisions), while others, including hotels and casinos, saw declines as regular customers avoided congestion. The last time the US hosted the world cup was 1994, and other studies have found limited economic impact of that event too. The Baade & Matheson (2004) paper referenced above found that the average host city for the 1994 world cup experienced a reduction in income of $712 million relative to predictions, and the overall negative impact on the US economy was $9.3 billion. In Baumann, Engelhardt and Matheson (2011), the authors found that contrary to optimistic pre-event forecasts, there was no statistically significant increase in overall employment or unemployment in host metropolitan areas during the tournament. Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures. Sources: FIFA, BNP Paribas estimates Fig. 1: World Cup matches distribution and maximum inflation effect – Brazil 2014 vs Mexico 2026 Premier sports events and inflation: The link between flagship global sporting events (such as soccer’s 2026 World Cup) and consumer prices is intuitive but often underestimated, we think. When a host is selected for a World Cup tournament or a round of Olympic Games, a multi-year economic cycle begins. Investment typically flows into venue construction, urban infrastructure, transportation networks and hospitality capacity. Workers are hired, wages tend to rise in construction and services jobs, and domestic demand is generally pulled forward. When the event itself arrives, the economy typically has already absorbed ample above-trend stimulus – and this shows up in prices. Economists call this the anticipation effect. Inflation does not spike on the day of a sporting event’s opening ceremony. Rather, it begins to build two to five years earlier, peaks around the event year and then fades. Crucially, there seems to be no lasting legacy inflation – once an investment cycle ends, price pressures normalize, typically with

n if the direction of travel remains data dependent. Third, we expect macro volatility itself to stay contained. Our economists look for core inflation to rise modestly to 2.6% oya over 4Q26-1Q27 before easing thereafter, while growth should improve over the coming months. With inflation expectations still well anchored, the hurdle for sustained policy shock should remain high. That said, there are still catalysts that can temporarily push implieds higher. A renewed energy shock or renewed geopolitical stress could reintroduce uncertainty around the ECB reaction function, particularly the trade-off between weaker growth and upside inflation. Separately, the US mid-term elections could trigger episodic risk premia and lift implieds at the margin. Overall, with a steadier policy path, fewer extreme outcomes, and smaller macro surprises, we expect implieds to grind lower and the surface to keep normalizing, with steepening across both expiries and tails. We do not, however, expect a full round-trip to the Jan-Feb lows. Ongoing Middle East uncertainty, even in a ceasefire regime, the higher level of mon- ey market yields, and elevated uncertainty around other DM central bank paths should keep the “resting level” of implieds higher than early-year averages. records.text: European Watch | 12 June 2026 3 through April) slowed further to 0.46% y/y, remaining comfortably within the SNB’s 0- 2% target range. Overall, Swiss underlying price dynamics still look subdued. After the April jump, foreign-produced inflation eased to 0.68% y/y from 0.87%, with CHF strength again partly offsetting higher energy prices. May was also an important month for rent indexation, a key transmission channel for SNB policy given the link between rents and mortgage rates. Rent inflation showed signs of plateauing, suggesting that the pass-through from past monetary easing may be nearing an end. Rates: constructive view & fine-tuned interventions With our economists’ projection that the SNB will keep policy rates at 0% until the end of 2027, we see the market pricing front-end rates too high, with almost a full hike priced in by March 2027. In terms of FX interventions, we see signs of the SNB having intervened in March, but with potentially more muted activity since. The SNB’s holding of foreign currency securities increased in March by €23bn CHF (though this may partly be explained by the strengthening of EURCHF over the month). Further, purchases of German debt securities from foreign official investors surged in March this year, with European countries outside the Eurozone being the primary investor group (45% of total net purchases), indicating the SNB may have taken part. records.text: 11 June 2026 Asia Local Markets Weekly Deutsche Bank AG/Singapore Page 11 India RBI measures point to 3Y CCS rally, with support near 6.0% RBI’s latest measures to attract FX inflows should have a direct impact on INR CCS, particularly in the 3Y tenor. n FCNR(B) deposit scheme appears attractive for both NRIs and foreign banks. Several Indian banks are offering around 6% on 3 to 5Y FCNR(B) deposits. With 3Y SOFR at around 4% and RBI absorbing the full FX hedging cost, this leaves roughly a 2% buffer for participation from NRIs and foreign banks. By our calculation, if NRIs apply around 10x leverage, the annualized return on initial capital could reach around 15%, making the scheme attractive enough to draw sizeable inflows. n Concessional FX swap window for PSU ECBs is also compelling. RBI is effectively offering a 3Y FX swap rate of around 1.5%, roughly 130bp below market levels. By our calculation, PSUs issuing ECBs and hedging via the RBI facility could achieve an all-in INR funding cost of around 6.5%, about 90bp lower than comparable onshore INR bond funding. Given PSUs account for around 37% of total ECB issuance, the lower hedging cost should incentivize them to front-load issuance during the concession window. If PSUs bring forward next year’s ECB issuance within the concession window, this could translate to around USD22bn of additional PSU ECB issuance. Reaching 2% inflation will not be an easy task. Not hiking means easing What matters for monetary policy is the real interest rate. The most important coefficient of the Taylor rule can testify: raise the nominal policy rate more than one-to- one relative to inflation. With rising inflation and inflation expectations, both realized and ex-ante real interest rates are in fact falling. This means that by not hiking rates in face of recurrent supply shocks, the Fed is effectively easing monetary policy. This easing in financial conditions can in turn contribute to global liquidity, worsening inflation dynamics including via wealth effects in the K-shaped economy. Short-term inflation expectations should matter after five years The textbook policy response is to look through supply shocks, waiting for the temporary increase in inflation to dissipate. Facing a temporary supply shock, monetary policy should react only if inflation expectations de-anchor or second round effects kick in, potentially contributing to the de-anchoring of inflation expectations. Beyond the single additional 25bp rate hikes we have forecasted in our base case for both central banks next week, we believe BI and the BSP would seek to cut rates next year. We expect the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the Bank of Thailand (BoT), not falling neatly into these two categories, to stay on hold through the rest of this year. For India, while growth is set to slow vs. the very strong growth of last year, inflation is set to rise: we expect CPI inflation to rise to 5% in FY27, 0.5pp higher from our earlier forecast. Much of this uptick in inflation is likely to be driven by food and fuel prices, and we think pressures are not reflecting as yet to core CPI, allowing the RBI's MPC space to look through sharply higher inflation readings for now, before considering hikes in H1 27. In Thailand, the BoT is likely more concerned about subpar growth, and thus would look through higher inflation prints. For both of these central banks, their policy reaction functions are less sensitive towards both the FX and supply-driven CPI shocks. The ECB lowered its 2026 and 2027 GDP growth forecasts by 0.1pp to 0.8% and 1.2%, respectively. While the revised Eurostat estimate showed a 0.2% q/q contraction in Eurozone GDP in Q1 (due to a 12.1% q/q decline in Irish GDP), for the staff projections the ECB used a smoothed quarterly profile for Ireland, resulting in +0.2% q/q Eurozone GDP growth in Q1. According to the ECB, the downward revision largely reflects a weaker outlook for consumption amid higher inflation and a larger drag on real incomes. For 2028, the ECB now expects GDP growth of 1.5%, 0.1pp higher than in March, thanks to a recovery in real incomes as energy prices fall (Figure 1). The ECB also provided an update to its adverse and severe scenarios, first introduced in March, and added a“milder” scenario. Compared to the June baseline, the alternative scenarios differ in their assumptions about the size and persistence of the energy shock, the degree of uncertainty, and the strength of transmission to non-energy prices. Specifically, the adverse scenario assumes a sharper and more persistent increase in energy prices, with stronger indirect and second-round effects on inflation. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has announced that it will absorb the entire hedging costs for banks on fresh Foreign Currency Non-Resident (FCNR(B)) deposits in US dollars. These deposits are fixed-term bank deposits that can be opened in India by NRIs, OCIs, and PIOs. The facility will be available until October 16, 2026, for deposits mobilized by September 30, 2026. With this announcement, banks can save hedging costs of approximately 300bps and offer significantly higher interest rates on 3- to 5-year foreign currency deposits. To facilitate this, the RBI has exempted these deposits from the Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio requirements. Additionally, the RBI has relaxed rules to allow Indian banks to issue Standby Letters of Credit, enabling overseas banks to lend money to NRIs against their FCNR deposits and creating investment leverage opportunities. Both monetary and fiscal policy are likely to face big policy trade-offs as the impact from the Iran conflict materializes. Outlook disrupted by the conflict Pre-conflict, the UK economy was reasonably on track for decent growth and gradual return of inflation closer to target. The conflict will likely bring lower growth and higher inflation. Inflationary pressures are likely to intensify from the middle of the year when gas prices rise, and food price pressures materialize. Growth is likely to slow down, but perhaps not as much as feared, with a recession unlikely. The key concern, according to our speakers, is the emergence of slack in the labour market and flattening of real wages. Youth unemployment is a particular issue with weak demand but also supply weighed by ill health. Mixed views on the Bank of England (BoE) Views on Bank of England’s (BoE) policy response to the conflict were mixed. The convergence timeline will be formalized in autumn 2026, when the 2027 budget is submitted to parliament alongside an updated medium-term fiscal stability plan to be submitted to the European Commission by mid-October. That would leave the July/Sept OIS spread under flattening pressure and conversely the Sept/Nov OIS spread under steepening pressure. This all presupposes that the MPC does not yet feel ready to push back on overall market pricing. Figure 4 shows evolution of the probability distribution of 1m OIS rates out of the Dec 2026 MPC meeting taken from rate option pricing. When compared to February, the modal outcome has shifted rightward (ie, higher rates) and the right-hand tail has got fatter, implying a higher probability is being attached to higher rates than lower rates. Another strong indicator to buy the dip is VRP , i.e. volatility risk premium. This indicator requires that the spread of VIX against exponentially weighted realized volatility is exceeded by two standard deviations. The backtest is shown in Figure 3. Holding realized volatility constant, this would require VIX to spike to 29.6 (from 21.3) to trigger. Of course, holding realized volatility constant when VIX is moving up is almost certainly wrong, suggesting that even higher VIX levels may be required to trigger. We therefore are not (yet) tempted to buy the dip. Globally Korea is closest but also did not trigger. VRP does not only work in the US, but also in most other countries, even though triggers are often coming in the same episodes, making the back tests not fully independent. At this stage other markets also do not trigger, though. Korea comes closest, but with the current realized volatility, implied vols are not high enough there, either. Prepared for Cayla Buettner

records.text: y’s convergence story and investor appeal. The recent escalation in the Middle East, including the Iran war, has introduced a more uncertain inflation outlook. The National Bank of Georgia (NBG) responded with a 25bp hike, signalling a cautious, data-dependent stance going forward. Policymakers appear particularly focused on measures of sticky inflation, which will be key in shaping the next steps in the cycle. Despite external volatility, domestic fundamentals remain solid. Large-scale investment projects led by the United Arab Emirates (UAE)’s Emaar Properties in Batumi and Tbilisi are now underway, supporting medium-term growth prospects. The banking system continues to demonstrate stability, while access to long-term gas contracts has insulated the economy from direct spillovers from higher regional gas prices. That said, the oil price shock has had a mixed impact. Higher oil prices have weighed on the current account and growth dynamics, although this has been partially offset by stronger demand in key trading partners (many of which are oil exporters) as well as improved export prices following disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz. On the FX side, the Georgian Lari (GEL) appears broadly fairly valued. The central bank continues to intervene opportunistically, focusing on reserve accumulation, with reserves currently at around 115% of adequacy metrics. Market access remains robust, as reflected in the recent Eurobond issuance, which was heavily oversubscribed (5.5x).

ECB: certain near-term action, uncertain path ahead There was broad consensus around a June rate hike by the European Central Bank (ECB), but the outlook beyond that remains uncertain. Discussions suggest that ECB concerns from the ongoing Iran conflict are fully focused on inflation rather than real economy. As such, in a scenario of prolonged conflict and sustained energy price pressures, inflation containment is expected to take priority over recession risks. Client expectations generally point to at least one additional rate hike after June, although expert discussions indicate that a single-hike scenario cannot be ruled out. At the same time, given current price levels, weakening economic conditions, and already tight credit standards, the overall hiking cycle is expected to be shorter and less aggressive than in 2022. However, we think it is useful to tell markets that the Fed could adjust policy based on incoming data and how it moves the committee's outlook, as well as the balance of risks. In other words, the Fed can change policy either because its forecast of the economy changes or because its view around the distribution of outcomes around its baseline has changed. We think this is useful information to retain in the statement. Striking paragraph four, in our view, would not amount to much. We see it as largely boilerplate language that is not entirely essential in understanding any policy decision or the Fed's reaction function. Nonetheless, we cannot rule out that the incoming chair will be more aggressive in his trimming of the statement and see this as a risk to our baseline expectation. Riksbank: hawkish hold in the price At its last meeting in May, the Riksbank adjusted its language in a slightly more hawkish direction. In contrast to March — when risks were still seen as two-sided and the policy rate path was left unchanged, signalling no hikes through the end of the year under the baseline — the focus this time was primarily on upside inflation risks. That said, the Board also acknowledged that below-target inflation and weaker-than-expected activity provide scope to remain patient. Interestingly, it refrained from explicitly commenting on whether the March policy rate path still held. In our view, this likely reflects a lack of a strong majority within the Board, with differing positions at the time — as also alluded to by Per Jansson in the minutes. records.text: US Economics Weekly12 June 2026 ab 23 Existing home sales rise but still lackluster Existing home sales rose 130K to 4.17 million (saar) in May, ahead of consensus (4.07 million) but closer to our estimate (4.12 million). Over the 12 months ending in May, existing home sales were up 3.2%. While the May data shows some improvement, and marks the highest level of sales since December, the series has bounced sideways at a low level lately. Inventories fell in May, with existing homes for sale down 22K to 1.47 million in May, or 4.3 months' supply at the current sales pace (down from 4.5 months' supply in April). That said, inventories remained within the tight, elevated range observed in the past year. Within the rates market, interest in the topic has mostly centred on how Dutch PFs’ existing fixed-income portfolios may need to be adjusted during the transition, with potential for significant reduction in longer-dated duration (see Flow expectations update – take 2, dated 21 November 2025). We believe potential transition flows remain an important theme for the rates market and can contribute to curve steepening and tenor-basis widening (see Enter 10y20y €STR/6s wideners and Re-entering long-end steepeners, dated 9 March and 8 April, respectively). However, with analysis surrounding the transition itself seeming close to saturation, we attempt to look beyond that, focusing on interest-rate hedging dynamics within the new CDC system . We think the Fed will continue to expect modestly above-trend growth and a stable unemployment rate. However, we think the Fed will revise higher again its outlook for headline and core PCE inflation, in favor of Q4/Q4 rates of inflation of 3.4% and 3.0%, respectively, up 0.7pp and 0.3pp, respectively versus March. As a result, we now expect the median target range for the federal funds rate to end the year at 3.50-3.75%, in line with the removal of the easing bias. In the dot plot, we see up to four dots calling for a rate hike in 2026 with these submissions potentially coming from Reserve Bank Presidents Logan, Hammack, Musalem, and Schmid. We doubt all four put in a hike in 2026 and think the actual number will be 2- 3 dots for a target range of 3.75-4.0% this year. In the other direction we see a maximum of 2 dots forecasting one 25bp rate cut in 2026 (potentially Governor Bowman and Chair Warsh).

Q7: What are the implications for Indonesian government bonds (IndoGBs)? “BI refraining from buying bonds” – seems to be the new message. If the ECB were to skip July and things evolved very positively in the run-up to the September meeting (probably more than in the milder scenario), it could be done at that point. Where do we go next? As a reminder, our expectation, with low conviction, is that the ECB will deliver another hike in July. And the conclusion from today is that July is live, but it will depend on the urgency generated by energy prices when we get there; otherwise, it will deliver in September. At the same time, the latest inflation print increases the likelihood of July if some of the move in Services proves not to be temporary. We think that cuts will need to follow, eventually. Our macro view holds firm: the path to sub-2% inflation is delayed, but all macro ingredients remain in play: a shallow recovery at unspectacular levels, with a very fragile and non-inflationary labour market, suboptimal fiscal policy, and central bank policy that always errs on the tight side. ECB: certain near-term action, uncertain path ahead There was broad consensus around a June rate hike by the European Central Bank (ECB), but the outlook beyond that remains uncertain. Discussions suggest that ECB concerns from the ongoing Iran conflict are fully focused on inflation rather than real economy. As such, in a scenario of prolonged conflict and sustained energy price pressures, inflation containment is expected to take priority over recession risks. Client expectations generally point to at least one additional rate hike after June, although expert discussions indicate that a single-hike scenario cannot be ruled out. At the same time, given current price levels, weakening economic conditions, and already tight credit standards, the overall hiking cycle is expected to be shorter and less aggressive than in 2022. Payroll growth has reaccelerated, with the three month average rising to around 188k, a clear improvement relative to last year and stronger than both our expectations and likely those of the Fed. This strength should alleviate concerns about downside risks to the labor market and reinforce the shift in the balance of risks toward inflation. At the same time, the unemployment rate remains low and broadly stable at around 4.3%. The key question is whether labor markets will tighten further, as in our demand push scenario. That, in turn, depends on the extent to which higher energy prices weigh on activity. The impact of oil shocks typically happens with a lag, suggesting some risk of a slowdown ahead. However, if that deceleration does not materialize and payroll growth remains around 100k—well above our estimated breakeven pace of roughly 50k—we would expect continued downward pressure on the unemployment rate. records.text: 16 Global Economic Weekly | 12 June 2026 Sub-Saharan Africa LIC DSA reform: towards a more holistic framework Discussions around the reform of the International Monetary Fund (IMF)’s Low-Income Country Debt Sustainability Analysis (LIC DSA) point to a shift toward a more integrated approach to debt risks, although key parameters remain under consultation. The IMF and the World Bank published the Background Note on Friday 2nd of June 2026. The reform will introduce a more holistic framework, closer to the Middle-Income Countries’ Sovereign Risk and Debt Sustainability Framework (SRDSF). The revised framework appears to add a stronger layer on domestic debt while maintaining the emphasis on external debt. The framework would drop one external debt burden indicator, Present Value (PV) of debt-to-exports, and introduce new overall public debt indicators including Gross Financing Needs to Gross Domestic Product (GFN-to-GDP) and interest-to-revenue excluding grants. This revamp is meant to reflect a structural shift in LIC debt profiles, which were predominantly external a decade ago but are now increasingly domestic. As a result, countries where domestic debt has risen sharply could face stronger risk signals under the revised framework. This is particularly relevant for several frontier markets where domestic financing has expanded rapidly, including Senegal, parts of Economic and Monetary Community of Central Africa (CEMAC), and Kenya. At the same time, market -based inflation expectations have edged higher, with Bloomberg data indicating that Q3 2026 expectations in most EM economies still run above central bank targets (Figure 1). However, the gap between market- implied one-year rates and estimated neutral rates suggests policy is not overly loose in most cases. Rates are generally at or below neutral, highlighting that central bank credibility remains broadly intact (Figure 2). Notable exceptions include Brazil and Colombia, where fiscal risk premia keep rates elevated; South Africa, due to a lower inflation target; and Mexico, where a more accommodative stance has slowed the anchoring of expectations. Overall, markets appear willing to look through near-term geopolitical shocks, reflecting sustained confidence in EM monetary frameworks. LatAm. To contextualise today's decision to hike by 25bp, we fed the ECB's latest staff projections into a suite of simple policy rules from the Fed. We then looked at what the various policy rules suggest the ECB should have done with policy rates in Q2 2026 given the staff expectations. It is important to note that these results are based on the staff projections for Q2-2026 (the current quarter) and do not account for inflation and activity developments further out in the forecast horizon. The results show that while a rate hike was universally prescribed, the recommended magnitude varied significantly depending on the rule's specification.. The 25bp hike delivered today appears most consistent with rules that either focus on core inflation or incorporate policy smoothing: n A Taylor rule using core inflation (green bar) prescribes a 30bp hike, broadly in line with the Governing Council's action. n Rules that smooth the policy path by considering past interest rate levels (orange bars) also suggest a moderate response, calling for hikes between 10-23bps.

records.text: ILS: Still the best tech hedge in FX. The Shekel has been on a round trip over the n last month—first appreciating to historically strong levels in May and then reversing that move quite sharply through June. We continue to think that most of the ILS price action can be explained by its high sensitivity to tech stocks, which have also been volatile. However, the more recent move likely also reflects BoI policy shifts, namely the decision to cut rates in May and to intervene in FX markets by buying Dollars for the first time since 2022. While uncertainty remains on the drivers of this intervention —partly because the central bank did not pre-announce them or a broader shift in FX policy—we have been arguing that policy pushback against a stronger ILS would likely grow as the Shekel reached historically strong levels, especially as competitiveness concerns come increasingly into focus. Therefore, with this overvaluation signal, positive carry for being short, and high beta to tech stocks, we have argued that the Shekel is an attractive hedge for portfolios highly levered to the performance of the technology sector, and can also serve as a funder for broader carry portfolios. The main risks to this view would be a substantial increase in local institutional investor’s hedge ratios (which we have not seen so far) or other local developments that could mute the Shekel’s beta to tech stocks. Investor Behavior: Rate Hikes May Also Weigh on Duration Demand In this section, we review investor behavior during rate hike cycles. It is often argued that when rate hikes proceed gradually, behind-the-curve dynamics lead to steepening pressure, whereas if the pace of rate hikes accelerates, expectations for long-term yields become more anchored, leading to flattening pressure. However, it should also be noted that rate hikes and rising yields can, in some cases, lead many investors to scale back their investments in JPY- denominated bonds. Below, we summarize investor behavior by type, and we would highlight that demand for JPY bonds from some overseas investors, banks, and life insurers is likely to remain sub- dued. Regardless of whether rate hikes are implemented, it appears difficult to expect a dra- matic improvement in JGB supply-demand conditions unless the macro environment shifts toward one characterized by increasing downside risks to growth and a pause in rate hikes. Specifically in equities, we would expect lower equity markets with an outperformance of defensive sectors and those that have a stronger beta to rates. Despite the relative performance across sectors, we think the recession scenario would require a decent correction in risk assets. On the rates side, we believe higher oil prices will lead to an initial bear flattening of yield curves before quickly reversing into a bull steepening as central banks deliver easing in a recession. The extent of the macro damage will determine where the easing cycle ultimately ends but we would anticipate policy rates to fall below neutral, making long duration and 1Yx1Y steepeners as the most attractive trades. In FX, the flight-to-quality dynamic would reignite the dollar smile, with broad support for the USD while bearish EM FX, especially the high yielders. Meanwhile in EM rates, we see an outperformance of low yielders and front-end flatteners, with central banks hiking first on financial stability risks, before easing. In both EM and DM credit, spreads would widen and we would hold a preference for High Grade over High Yield and favour US HG over European HG. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W keep page margin clear keep page margin clear 212/06/2026 Across the 12 domestic life insurers we monitor, domestic bond holdings total roughly JPY3.3trn. Although the direction of change varies by insurer, overall domestic bond exposure has reduced, especially to policy-reserve matching bonds (PRM bonds). At the same time, use of swaps for hedging is also declining. We think the sell-off reflects a need to dispose of low-coupon bonds that would otherwise require impairment (see Japan flow insight: Changing demand structure, dated 24 February 2026). Revisions to the impairment rules mean that a drop in book value to 50% no longer forces a sale of PRM bonds. Even before the change, some insurers announced they would hold PRM bonds to maturity to avoid impairment. Their continued disposal of the bonds therefore signals that life insurers find it rational to sell domestic bonds. As a result, despite the sharp rise in market rates, insurers’ interest-rate risk – as measured by economic equity value – has not deteriorated. On foreign bonds, life insurers’ investment in USD-denominated securities is picking up again. After a pronounced shift into EUR-denominated assets in the first half of last fiscal year, the size of the USD corporate bond market now suggests a pivot back toward USD. Next Thursday’s Makerfield by-election is a pivotal n moment in Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham’s path to a potential Labour party leadership contest, but we see the event risk for Sterling as being fairly narrow. Political and fiscal risk premium in the currency remains light on our measure, despite a Burnham-led government (and the associated risks of potential adjustments to the UK’s fiscal stance) now priced in prediction markets as more likely than not by year-end. Shifts in these odds have weighed on GBP in bouts over recent months rather than providing a sustained headwind even when prediction markets moved firmly towards Burnham in recent weeks (Exhibit 4). To see premium expand again and weigh materially on Sterling, we think the onus is now either on an announcement of policy plans that lead markets to question the UK’s fiscal trajectory, or for political uncertainty to rise and linger for longer. And even under such a scenario, we expect other, more fundamental factors to continue to dominate price action. The evolution of the energy shock remains key to that. We continue to think the current window of unresolved energy supply risks and limited political premium priced in Sterling offers decent value in GBP downside versus terms of trade winners such as USD or AUD, but in our view these expressions are best suited to more tactical horizons or tail hedges. records.text: EM – LOC AL EY ES F OR A GLOBAL VI EW 310/06/2026 Lifecycle investing approach: Post-transition, Dutch PFs that have moved to the solidarity contract will follow a new ‘lifecycle investing’ framework that aligns asset-allocation with members’ age-related risk tolerance. Under this approach, the youngest cohorts, typically those under 45, are allocated a substantial share of equities to capture the long-term growth premium that equities historically provide. As participants age, the allocation gradually de-risks: mid-career members see a progressive reduction in risky asset weighting, complemented by a rising share of fixed-income assets and interest rate swap hedges. This strategy aims to balance the trade-off between potential returns and risk management, ensuring that retirement savings are optimised for each life stage . Figure 5 illustrates an example of lifecycle allocation under the solidarity contract. Leverage is possible as the current borrowing restriction is absent in the new pension contract, allowing the total weighting of the investments to add up to more than 100% of the total invested capital. Indeed, most pension schemes we analysed have used a weighting of over 100% in the youngest group’s return portfolio allocation . Our analysis suggests an increase in capital outflows. This is evidenced by a widening gap between official customs trade data and BoP recorded imports—indicative of import over- invoicing—and corroborated by rising E&O in Vietnam’s BoP. The ongoing rise in custom import growth YTD would suggest further outflows remain. Combined with persistent equity outflows, these pressures risk tipping Vietnam’s overall BoP into deficit. Based on historical cycles, a $10bn BoP deficit has tended to correspond with roughly 4% VND depreciation against the USD. A significant offset is Vietnam’s recent upgrade by FTSE Russell from Frontier to Secondary Emerging Market status. This makes the country eligible for inclusion in key FTSE Global Equity Index Series, such as the FTSE All-World and FTSE Emerging Markets indices, which will create a direct demand impulse for the dong. We estimate potential total inflows of ~$6bn. Of this, ~$1.5bn is expected from passive funds. The remaining ~$4.5bn from active managers is discretionary and may already be partially positioned. Index inclusion will begin on 21 September 2026, with passive fund flows phased in over four quarterly tranches (10%, 20%, 35%, and 35%) through September 2027. records.text: Global Economic Viewpoint | 11 June 2026 15 Iran: Hormuz for Hormuz deal – so close, yet so far Opposition among key domestic stakeholders as well as recent tit-for-tat between Israel/US and Iran could push the timeline for conclusion of US-Iran negotiations further out. This could also harden the Iranian negotiation position. Differences remain in regard to linking regional ceasefires, nuclear matters, sanctions relief and status of Hormuz Strait/Hormuz blockade in a potential phased deal. The US position appears to have softened in comparison to initial demands. Iranian leadership pronouncements suggest a desire to maintain deterrence and prevent a repeat of the war. The market consensus appears to be relatively benign, with an agreement and Hormuz re-opening over the summer once market pressures re-assert themselves and push parties, particularly the US, to compromise. The better-than-expected behavior of oil prices reflects the drawdown of commercial and government inventories in the developed and developing world (particularly China), reduced Chinese crude oil imports, higher US crude oil exports, General Licenses (GLs) on Russian and Iranian oil-at-sea, as well as some demand destruction. In the absence of acute market pressure, both parties are likely to continue running down the clock at the risk of going over the oil cliff. records.text: Solvency-II related changes compared to before. To recap, the proposed amendments to Solvency-II have now been approved and will apply from 30 January 2027 (see here). In our 2026 Outlook, we discussed the key changes related to the i) RFR curve extrapolation methodology – a phased in implementation over the next five years but overall supportive of wider spreads; ii) V ola- tility Adjustment: the introduction of the Credit Spread Sensitivity Ratio (CSSR) in the V ol- atility Adjustment would penalize insurance companies who use covered bonds and deriva- tives to manage the Asset/Liability duration mismatch. However, there is limited visibility on the extent of flows resulting from these changes given the changes in discounting curves are implemented over a long period and similarly the changes to volatility adjustment can be managed over time. In addition, we also highlight the introduction of the First Smoothing Point (FSP) in the calculation of the discounting curve mentioned above as opposed to using the Last Liquid Point (LLP). Specifically, unlike LLP which was fixed at 20Y , FSP is dynamic and will be determined annually by EIOPA. The FSP rate will be updated monthly but the FSP point will be itself determined annually using predetermined rules. Specifically, the FSP is defined asthe longest maturity for which two criteria are fulfilled: i) it is DLT (Deep, Liquid, and Transparent maturity), and ii) the percentage of outstanding instruments of that or a longer maturity

All three World Cup venues in Mexico existed before the country was selected to be a host – the Estadio Azteca required only refurbishment, while Monterrey’s Estadio BBVA (2015) and Guadalajara’s Estadio Akron (2010) were already fully functional – so the multi-year construction boom that accounts for most of a full host’s inflation premium is largely absent here. Besides group-stage fixtures, Mexico will stage only two more matches: one round-of-32 and a round-of-8. Hence, the anticipation arc the model identifies for full hosts never really forms. Instead, there’s a short, demand-side tourism pulse concentrated in three cities around the time of the matches, which is why the cumulative impact stays at ~0.3pp, with less than 0.1pp in 2026. It remains to be seen to what extent the relative resilience in April – which, according to PMIs, likely extended into May – reflects stockpiling behaviour in anticipation of further price increases and broader supply disruptions. In Germany, for instance, the boost to manufacturing new orders in March appears to have mostly reversed in April (-3.8% m/m), driven by core orders (excluding large-ticket items). Abstracting from monthly volatility, there are still no clear signs of a pickup in manufacturing demand, which continues to hover around the subdued levels observed since early 2024. Türkiye: Geopolitics delays disinflation, FX stability holds Hande Kucuk MLI (UK) hande.kucuk@bofa.com The tone on Türkiye was cautious, with the disinflation process increasingly challenged by geopolitical developments, even as the monetary stance remains tight in response to rising inflation risks. Higher oil prices linked to the Middle East conflict are feeding into energy and food inflation, pushing headline prints higher and weighing on expectations, with risks tilted to the upside amid potential second round effects. At the same time, moderating domestic demand and easing inertia across services subgroups suggest that disinflation could resume once the energy shock dissipates, albeit at a slower pace than envisaged pre-conflict.

At the last meeting, the Fed noted that "The Committee is attentive to the risks to both sides of its dual mandate. While improvements in efficiency might lead to slight increases, more substantial growth would require greater rig activity—which seems unlikely in the near future. Even if we account for a six-month lag before new drilling impacts production, major output gains appear limited before the end of the year. We also expect supply growth from Latam, Canada and elsewhere but it is mainly due to the ramp-up of projects already in development, not a price response. Our Latam supply growth is 0.8Mb/d this year with Brazil adding 0.5Mb/d from new FPSOs at Buzios and Mero, coming onstream ahead of schedule and running smoothly. Guyana is seeing more production from the Stabroek FPSO pipeline, including Yellowtail last year, Uaru this year, and Whiptail next year. Another view was that the more persistent the shock is, the more pressure there will be on the BoE to hike, though they would do so reluctantly. Those who believed that the BoE could hike noted that, in the near term, no action is likely. However, they noted that pressure on the BoE to hike could rise in September once inflation rises in July, assuming the energy price rise in persistent (and scenarios could be tweaked to reflect a more persistent shock). Action from other central banks could also influence the reaction function of the BoE. But there was broad based agreement that the BoE is unlikely to cut this year, even if the conflict resolves. Fiscal challenges are likely to be high Speakers agreed that fiscal challenges are likely to be high, no matter who is in charge. There is limited headroom within the current fiscal rules, with the conflict implying a £10-15bn hit already to the headroom. At the same time, pressures to provide energy support to lower income households will likely rise, along with pressures on defence spending, unprotected departments and volatility in gilt yields. The government would likely require a credible balance between short-term fiscal spending and medium-term fiscal consolidation. On this simple analysis, the broad decline in credit risk helps explain the lion share of the compression in spreads since 2022. Improvement in the liquidity characteristics of EU bonds are meaningful too, contributing by about 15bps tightening from the wides (Exhibit 10). If the bid-ask spread of EU bonds tightened further to levels consistent with the size of EU debt outstanding, our betas indicate this could be worth as much as 4-5bps in EU-Bund compression. Since 2021, EU bonds have gone from outperforming our simple fitted value on credit and liquidity to a modest underperformance, this suggests another factor could be playing a role in keeping EU spreads relatively wide. Given the stock of EU debt increasing by a factor of ten over the corresponding period, elevated bond supply is a reasonable candidate explanation behind this underperformance. But this is difficult to corroborate with data. In fact, we find that gross duration supply over a given period is a poor guide to EU bond performance vs core/semi core peers over the same period (Exhibit 11). A more convincing explanation may simply be that the EU trades in line with average Euro area aggregate fundamentals, rather than its AAA rating. Systemic vs idiosyncratic Finally, it’s worth mentioning that all the previous analysis , which is based on recent betas vs other correlated market variables, assumes that EGB spreads’ variation over the past three months can be entirely attributed to systemic (exogenous) and not idiosyncratic factors. Without a doubt, exogenous factors have been the main drivers of EGB spreads during this period, but at the same time we have seen some headlines about the political situation in Italy after PM Meloni lost th e recent referendum while in France we had some reports about a worsenin g outlook for next year’s deficit. These events might help explain the relative cheapening of these two countries’ spreads relative to their peers over the past three months. On top of that, the ECB already hiked once, and might hike some more in th e months ah ead which could have repercussions for countries with high annual refinancing needs and vulnerable debt sustainability dynamics. All this to say that when exogenous drivers dominate it’s useful to run all these beta-based analyses but at the same time we should keep an eye on for idiosyncratic drivers or different sensitivities across countries. records.text: We expect the measures announced by the RBI to generate USD70–80bn worth of inflows in the second half of this year. For context, India's current account deficit in H2 2025 was USD28bn. Even assuming a higher deficit in 2026 due to increased oil prices, these inflows are likely to more than cover the shortfall. As a result, the RBI's headline foreign exchange reserves would increase, while its net reserves (adjusted for forward book) should remain relatively stable. With higher headline reserves over the next 3–5 years, the RBI would then have more ammunition to intervene in the FX market if needed. This does not necessarily mean the RBI will actively push the USDINR exchange rate lower from current levels. However, we think this scenario would likely work to cap USDINR upside and prevent a significant depreciation of the currency. We therefore expect the INR to outperform other regional currencies, and its own forward rates, as the increased reserves provide a buffer against potential downward pressure on the currency. We also expect the realized volatility in USDINR to come down as the RBI can become active on both sides. If the USDINR goes higher due to depreciation pressure, it can stop the move by selling US dollars with these new flows and then buy US dollars if the USDINR comes down to recoup the FX reserves lost in the last few quarters. On 10 June, the BoJ revealed that Governor Ueda would be hospitalized for around two weeks. He will only convey his views in writing and will be absent from the meeting itself. Voting will therefore be conducted by the remaining eight members. Deputy Governor Himino will serve as acting chair, while Deputy Governor Uchida will hold the press conference. If the vote is split 4-4, Acting Chair Deputy Governor Himino will make the final decision, so the likelihood of disruption to policy decisions appears extremely low. India has been experiencing currency depreciation pressure due to capital outflows from equities, exacerbated by a deteriorating current account balance caused by higher oil prices and a decline in the Indian IT sector amid the global evolution of Artificial Intelligence (AI). In response, the RBI announced several measures last week to combat currency depreciation, including: Attractive FCNR(B) deposits: The RBI will fully cover the foreign exchange hedging costs for banks that raise fresh 3-5 year Foreign Currency Non-Resident (FCNR) deposits. Bond access and lower taxes: The RBI has expanded the universe of securities under the Fully Accessible Route to include all new issuances of 15-, 30-, and 40- year government securities. We expect housing starts and permits both fell modestly in May, and the housing market index likely edged down in June. We expect industrial production rose 0.3% in May, with assembly schedules suggesting flat motor vehicles and parts production. Import price data will round out our core PCE tracking for May. records.text: South Africa slowed by 37bps in May, though the annual rate rose to 5.81% from 4.35%. The disinflation trend was interrupted in April by higher energy prices. Core inflation is edging up, while softe r food prices are partly offsetting the energy shock. SARB delivered the widely expected 25bps hike to remain vigilant on inflation risks and is likely to retain a hawkish bias. In Poland, PriceStats data show a sharp slowdown in inflation in May on both a monthly and a nnual basis. Monthly inflation fell to -0.29% from 1.03%, while annual inflation eased to 5.03% from 5.98% in April. Inflation expectations remain well anchored, with the market pricing policy rates near neutral over the next year. Inflation in Turkey remains highly sensitive to oil price moves. Unlike in Poland, energy shocks in Turkey feed quickly into core inflation because policy credibility is weaker and inflation remains high. M onthly PriceStats fell to 1.55% in May from 2.81% in April, bringing annua l inflation down slightly to 32.95% from 33.06%. CBRT responded with FX intervention and tighter policy settings, and we expect its hawkish stance to continue. Emerging Asia. In South Korea, online inflation moderated by 28bps to 0.25% in May. While headline inflation has picked up on higher energy prices and currency depreciation, the rise in core inflation has been more limited, and inflation expectations were well anchored earlier this year. If that is the case we would expect the FOMC to assume three 25 bp rate hikes as a base case. That would essentially undo the rate cuts from last year due to the new shock and three hikes puts the FOMC in a better position if four or five are deemed to be needed. Of course how equity markets react, given the reliance of the expansion on AI investment and its wealth creation could be an important consideration too. The timing depends somewhat on what Chair arrives. A hawkish Chair Warsh and rate hikes could be a fast pivot following disappointing July/August inflation data, with warning or even hikes beginning at the September FOMC. However our guess for a more probable timeframe would be a December FOMC meeting, after the mid term elections, that assumes three 25 bp rate hikes are appropriate in 2027. As a base case we think the FOMC remains on prolonged hold. But they may need to raise rates. One reason a central bank raises rates is credibility. records.text: M Idea 2 Smoothing over the last six months, breakeven still looks like 50k per month Over the last several months, payroll increases have been above our estimate of labor supply growth. We estimate the breakeven pace for payrolls consistent with an unchanged unemployment rate to be 50k per month. With the faster payrolls pace of the last several months, why hasn’t the unemployment rate fallen? And if payroll strength continues, will labor supply be sufficient? In the past three months, payrolls averaged 188k per month and the unemployment rate inched down 0.14 pct pt; the combination suggests a breakeven pace of 110k—well above our 50k estimate. However, in the prior three months payrolls fell -4k per month on average and the unemployment rate fell 0.10 pct pt, consistent with a breakeven pace of - 50k. If the household survey and establishment survey were perfectly calibrated, then the unemployment rate would have risen more in the three months through February, then fallen more in the three months through May, all to end up at the same, current 4.3% rate. Six-, nine-, and 12-month comparisons make for a cleaner assessment, and they look consistent with the 50k breakeven we have estimated. For example, over the past 12 months, payrolls have risen at a 42k monthly pace, the unemployment rate has inched up 0.05 pct pt, and we calculate the observed breakeven pace at 48k. records.text: Outlook for the economy and prices (last updated 12 June) In the second preliminary estimate of Q1 GDP released by the Cabinet Office on 8 June, real growth was revised down to 1.8% q/q saar from an initial 2.1%. This was mainly due to capex adjustments (to 2.8% q/q saar from 1.1%), reflecting the findings of the corporate survey. However, as a broad range of other components underwent upward adjustment, the downward revision to real GDP growth was modest relative to market expectations. This strong Q1 result did not fully reflect the impact of Middle East tensions, which intensified from late February onward. Looking ahead, higher energy prices stemming from these developments will weigh on both consumption and capex. If supply constraints in products such as naphtha materialize, the impact could expand in a non-linear manner. That said, assuming tensions in the Middle East will gradually ease, we would expect firms to resume active investment aimed at rebuilding supply chains to cope with labor shortages, while consumption also recovers, supported by large wage hikes. From the H2 FY26 onward, the fiscal policy of the Takaichi administration, which is aiming for a high-pressure economy, is also expected to provide some support for growth. records.text: 3 Insights Information Classification: General About PriceStats PriceStats is a source of high frequency inflation information drawn from prices of over five million items sold by online retailers. The items include food, beverages, electronics, apparel, furniture, household products, prescription drugs and over-the-counter medicines. The prices are collated for all the countries we monitor to produce individual Country Inflation Series. Country Inflation Series detect changes in inflation trends with real-time data. We publish the indices with a lag of three business days; they are direct reflections of prices of real products on sale at online retailers in each country. Country Inflation Series are not seasonally adjusted and are not designed to match official data. Whether S&P 500 valuations revert toward their long-term average or prove structurally higher going forward will depend in large part on the trajectory of corporate profitability. Based on our macro model, every 1 percentage point change in S&P 500 ROE is associated with a change of roughly 1x in S&P 500 P/E. Within SARB’s Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), the debate narrowed to hold versus a 25bp hike (with 50bp discussed but ultimately unnecessary). This reflects that, unlike the 2022 cycle, real rates are already restrictive, reducing the need for aggressive tightening. The inflation outlook is shaped more by price pressures than supply constraints for now. However, risks could build if elevated diesel and fertiliser costs lead to a low planting season, raising the risks of higher food inflation in 2027, compounded by potential El Niño weather disruptions. In the near term, services inflation remains elevated, driven mainly by housing and medical insurance costs, but has not yet broadened into a generalised second round dynamic. Inflation expectations are still relatively well anchored (peaking at c3.5%), and wage pressures remain contained overall. The SARB’s baseline Quarterly Projection Model (QPM) path implies a near-term hike followed by easing later in the year, but this reflects model mechanics (Taylor rule dynamics) rather than firm guidance. Perceptions for TRS are nuanced and follow a tiered logic. These instruments are broadly accepted when used as a temporary liquidity bridge in credits under pressure, such as Angola, but are viewed far more critically in higher-risk sovereigns like Senegal, where default risks are perceived to be materially higher. The bottom line is, we can see the ECB hiking again in September, but we don’t see the ECB hiking beyond 2.50%. ECB staff macroeconomic projections Growth As in March, the ECB presented a baseline scenario alongside alternative, adverse and severe scenarios. This time, it also added a milder scenario. The key determinant across the scenarios is the assumed path for oil prices. Baseline: only a marginal downgrade. In the new baseline scenario, oil prices are based on market expectations at the time the ECB finalised its projections, with oil at USD 103/b in Q3. Under this baseline, the ECB revised growth down only marginally: by 0.1pp in both 2026 and 2027, to 0.8% and 1.2%, respectively, while leaving 2028 unchanged. The downgrade reflects the persistence of the war in Iran, with domestic demand expected to suffer more than previously assumed because of higher inflation, weaker real disposable income, greater uncertainty and lower confidence. The ECB has also revised the fiscal stance for 2026, which is now slightly looser than projected in March (-0.5pp of GDP rather than -0.3pp of GDP). The slightly looser stance in 2026, followed by a partial reversal in 2027, is mainly driven by temporary energy support measures adopted since the start of the war in the Middle East. records.text: ouncements were made by Bank Indonesia and the Ministry of Finance? Prior to the meeting, BI emphasized its intention to enhance monetary and fiscal coordination with the MOF. Notably, both authorities have agreed to allow market forces to determine the yields of Indonesian government bonds (SBNs), by ceasing to purchase these bonds. Furthermore, BI will gradually sell its existing holdings of SBNs, while also increasing the yields on its own instruments, such as the Surat Berharga Bank Indonesia (SRBI). The objective of these measures is to lift yields to a level that attracts foreign investors, as repeatedly emphasized by BI Governor Warjiyo, who has encouraged investors to purchase bonds due to their attractiveness now. Additionally, BI reaffirmed its commitment to maintaining ample liquidity and supporting money growth at a rate of 10%. To achieve this, BI has reintroduced weekly repo auctions with tenors of 3, 6, 9, and 12 months to inject liquidity into the market. Q7: What are the implications for Indonesian government bonds (IndoGBs)? “BI refraining from buying bonds” – seems to be the new message. This is the first time they have openly stated that they will allow bond yields to rise and will sell their IndoGB holdings over time. We believe this is a significant change in their stance, as previously BI had been buying IndoGBs from the market since 2020. Medium-term inflation outlook broadly unchanged The new round of conditional inflation forecasts is likely to convey the key message that the medium‑term outlook remains unchanged despite short‑lived price pressures. In March, SNB projections anticipated inflation at 0.5% yoy in both 2026 and 2027, and 0.6% in 2028. It is likely that the SNB will opt for only marginal revisions to the June projections, with the annual average little changed at 0.5% this year, 0.6% (+10bp) in 2027 and 0.6% in 2028. We think two elements will feature prominently next week: 1) the SNB’s willingness to look through temporary deviations from its 0-2% target band, and 2) essentially unchanged medium-term pressure. We see little case for near-term tightening Inflation risks from higher energy prices have led markets to rapidly reassess central- bank pricing, including for the SNB. Markets now price close to a full hike by March 2027. But inflation risks from energy should be balanced against FX risks from safe- haven flows. May inflation recap May’s headline CPI (+0.47% vs. +0.64% in April) was slightly softer than we expected, mostly a function of weaker food inflation (+0.16% vs. +0.50%) . records.text: Our thoughts on USD, CNY, GBP , JPY, NJA FX, CHF & ILS USD: Oil off the boil keeps the Dollar in a collar. We have been arguing recently n that the combination of two global themes—an AI boom and an energy supply bust—are both net positive for the Dollar, but strong cyclical forces and policy measures push in the other direction for key parts of the currency complex. That cyclicality, and the US’s relative isolation, keep the Dollar captive to ceasefire headlines, but we think the trendline keeps pointing higher in the near term as the fallout from a more sustained energy shortfall grows. At the same time, a growing realization of a smaller-than-expected oil deficit has helped keep growth expectations from diverging further even as the disruption drags on longer. In this context, we view the recent moves as trimming some of the dovish Dollar tail around next week’s FOMC, as pricing for the next few meetings now shows a more limited premium for hikes. But even beyond next week, we think more restrained energy moves limit the opportunity for USD volatility to climb out of the doldrums despite elevated macro uncertainty.
