That will be enough for the FOMC to more formally adopt a “neutral” stance in the post-meeting statement and for the median “dot” to project unchanged policy rates in 2026, but these hawkish developments are expected and priced-in. We see potential for Chair Warsh to dovishly surprise markets by suggesting that the Fed may return to cutting rates, emphasizing the lack of broad-based inflationary pressure in the economy. A key question is how strongly he points out that PCE inflation has become something of an outlier, having increased to a rate above 3%. He might mention, for instance, that trimmed-mean PCE has slowed to 2.3-2.4%, not too-far off target. It's also become increasingly widely acknowledged that AI-related prices are being overrepresented in PCE relative to CPI. That could give Warsh a reason to focus more on recently cooler core CPI readings than stronger PCE. Warsh will also likely echo Powell in pointing out that despite recently stronger job growth, wage growth has slowed and the labor market is not a source of inflationary pressure. records.text: 2 Global Economic Weekly | 12 June 2026 Global Letter Claudio Irigoyen BofAS Antonio Gabriel BofAS The Fed is passively easing policy With rising inflation and inflation expectations, both realized and ex-ante real interest rates are falling. By not hiking rates, the Fed is effectively easing monetary policy and contributing to loose financial conditions and high global liquidity. The textbook policy response is to look through supply shocks, as Team Transitory would argue, waiting for the temporary increase in inflation to dissipate. However, after five years of above-target inflation, and supply shocks that are becoming more frequent and persistent amid rising geopolitical tensions, sound risk management for monetary policy may advocate otherwise. Furthermore, the recent decomposition of inflation is bleak. The tailwind from housing will likely fade, leaving core services inflation at elevated levels. Unless core goods inflation somehow becomes negative, no cuts should be in sight from a normative point of view, even with a deal in Iran. We have been arguing that the economy doesn’t need further easing since well before the war. However, normative and positive economics do not always meet at the same corner. Supply shocks are becoming the new normal From Covid-related supply chain disruptions to the war in Ukraine, Houthi attacks in the red sea, the trade war, and the Iran war, supply shocks are becoming a perennial story. Going from these levels to 1.4-15mn b/d over the next 18-24 months seems feasible; however, converging to the pre-crisis levels of 3.0mn b/d would demand about USD10bn in investment per year over the next seven years, which would depend heavily on the political conditions in the country and potential additional changes to the legal framework, which are still uncertain. When thinking about the implications for the prospects for debt restructuring, we have to be cautious. While the reduction in the government's take due to the new hydrocarbons law may improve investment incentives, a potentially sharp decline of royalties and tax rates, as well as greater private participation that implies higher profit repatriation, could mean that higher oil exports do not translate proportionally into fiscal revenue. In Chile, the current account deficit should remain below the historical norm, even with oil prices still elevated. And that is what we got. The ECB delivered the well-telegraphed hike this week. And that came, also as expected, with no pre-commitment on the trajectory, a data-dependent approach, but still an implicit steer that absent very good news (on energy prices) or very bad news (on the economy), it is not done here. Indeed, Lagarde took us back to the watchers speech when she described three broad scenarios depending on the size and the persistence of the shock. And she implied that we are in a scenario that needs a measured response (not a forceful one). That, together with forecasts that include more than one hike, while still having inflation back at target, means the ECB is likely not done yet.

records.text: Japan Rates Weekly 12 June 2026 Citi Research 3 Can the BoJ sound hawkish? The BoJ is seen as certain to hike its policy rate to 1% and to announce it will pause reducing JGB purchase amounts from April 2027 at next week’s Monetary Policy Meeting. Governor Kazuo Ueda is not expected to attend, but this should not affect the debate or actual decisions. The focus will be on whether the policy board member T oichiro Asada will vote against a rate hike. If he does, we think it will likely be seen as representative of the Takaichi government’s dovish stance. Junko Nakagawa’s term on the Policy Board will end on June 29 and she will be replaced from the next meeting by Ayano Sato. This means the market will be conscious of the possibility that there may be two votes opposing rate hikes to 125bp or 150bp. Presumed pressure from the government could cause the market to price in greater difficulty in hiking the policy rate in the second half of next year. However, yen depreciation could accelerate if there is a dovish decision regarding balance sheet policy or if there is a reduced outlook for rate hikes. The forex rate, which depends on US interest rates, will remain a key determinant of whether an early rate hike is needed in September or October. Intervention to buy the yen could continue until this situation stabilizes, but if the US economy remains robust the Takaichi government would likely be forced to accept a rate hike. Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham is standing as the Labour candidate and if he were to win the by-election, he would become an MP and be eligible to stand in a Labour leadership contest. The latest Survation poll from 4 th June suggests a lead for Labour ahead of Reform (Labour 49%, Reform 39%). - A Burnham win would open the door to either a coronation (whereby Burnham becomes Labour leader, without a contest) or a leadership contest (which would likely take a few weeks). In such a leadership contest, according to unconfirmed media reports, Andy Burnham would likely be the soft left candidate, potentially with Health Secretary Wes Streeting and PM Starmer (if he decides to run) also potential challengers. In such a leadership challenge, Survation poll (30 th April- 5th May) suggests that Burnham is viewed as favourite to win.

Moreover, if the Middle East situation stabilizes, uncertainty over the outlook for economic activity should diminish, likely prompting the BoJ to become even more conscious of upside inflation risks. In recent years, firms have become more accustomed to passing higher costs through to prices, and the BoJ appears increasingly wary that the mechanism through which higher oil prices feed into inflation has strengthened versus the past. As a result, after a June hike, we think the BoJ will be willing to accept somewhat shorter intervals between hikes, and will make additional moves in October and April 2027 in line with our projections prior to the conflict. Week ahead The week ahead brings the results of the June BoJ monetary policy meeting and Deputy Governor Uchida’s press conference on 16 June, followed by the release of May nationwide CPI data on the 19th. Although a 25bp rate hike at the June meeting has already been reported, the inflation risk premium remains the main theme in the JGB market via fluctuations in the term premium, so the focus is on the BoJ’s stance toward future inflationary pressures. After the 9 June Nikkei report on the BoJ rate hike, the term premium declined somewhat, and one possible factor may have been expectations that the rate hike would restrain inflation. With the BoJ’s stance toward future inflation serving as a major short-term driver of yield moves, Deputy Governor Uchida’s press conference will be closely watched. In addition, the nationwide core CPI to be released after the BoJ meeting could also become a driver of yield moves through market expectations for the inflation risk premium if it deviates from consensus forecasts; an upside surprise could trigger a short-term rise in the inflation risk premium. The JGB purchase plan from April 2027 onward will be another focus of the June BoJ meeting. It has already been reported that monthly purchases will be kept unchanged at JPY2.1trn from April 2027 onward. The spread signal is calculated as the ratio of the current spread relative to the prior one-year median spread. The values are then smoothed using a 20-day moving average. For example, a multiple of 1 indicates that the current average spread is equal to the historical median spread for that currency pair, whereas a multiple reading of 2 indicates that the current average spread for that given currency pair is twice as wide as its historical median. Turbulence is a price-based measure of the joint unusualness of G10 currency returns. It captures spikes in volatility in individual market components as well as correlation breakdowns – atypical co-movements – between these components. Just as its inventory build-up had cushioned the price drop last year, China has capped the upside this time. Commercial inventories have played a part too though and the market will not be able to rely on these indefinitely. We estimate that the supply loss remains close to 15Mb/d and that if we do see not an improvement, US commercial inventories could approach more critical levels by end July. Hormuz still the key driver for scenarios but not completely binary We continue to see risk to the upside as long as flows via Hormuz are severely reduced. An extended disruption beyond July could still see prices rise to $150+/bbl. Conversely, were the Strait to reopen fully in the coming days, then we could see a sharper drop in prices, consistent with our previous base case. There are also scenarios in which prices could stay close to current levels for longer. Firstly, a deal/reopening is not completely binary: there is a situation in which flows remain below normal as Iran retains some control while we could see a further increase in flows without a deal. Secondly, China could reduce imports further for longer, reducing the pressure on oil markets. records.text: 11 June 2026 Asia Local Markets Weekly Deutsche Bank AG/Singapore Page 5 Macro Strategy Shifting gears Just this past week, the Korean authorities have launched investigations into unfair trading and speculative activities, and warned of the spillover from NDF markets; Indian authorities have announced several measures to attract more foreign capital; and Indonesian authorities have done a surprise off cycle hike. Are these effective as circuit breakers? Beyond the immediate position adjustment, while currencies are cheap to fair value in all three, policy efforts in Korea should have additional tailwinds from an increasingly hawkish stance (even if well priced) and a big stock of under-converted exporter earnings. Resident equity outflows have been less a headwind for KRW of late; and the changes to NPS hedging ratio targets should also work in its favour. The steepest hurdle though for KRW continues to be the rebalancing/hedging by offshore holders of Korean equities, which is driving the delta on the BoP math in the short term. Policy efforts in both India and Indonesia have included cheapening the cost of currency hedging for offshore capital in an effort to rebalance the short-term BoP math. We took this subject up in our recent US Economics Weekly: Are neutral rates moving structurally higher? Where the rubber meets the road: Participants' assessments of uncertainty and risks around their economic projections In our view, committee members' views about the balance of risks are as important, if not more important, than the baseline outlook. After all, the Fed cut rates primarily on concerns about downside risks to labor markets outweighing upside risk to inflation. Who's to say this cannot happen in reverse? In other words, members who project inflation to moderate in their modal scenario may see risks to the outlook for inflation as skewed to the upside and risks to the outlook for unemployment skewed to the downside. If so, then the committee could move toward risk-management rate hikes later this year while still projecting inflation to moderate in the modal outlook. In March of this year, 16 of 19 participants saw risks to the unemployment rate as weighted to the upside against none who saw risks weighted to the downside. We think this changes in June, but still see more participants concerned about high unemployment rates than low unemployment rates. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear 412/06/2026 Q8: What are the implications for Indonesian government bonds (IndoGBs)? The new messaging appears to make clear that BI will refrain from buying bonds, This is the first time it has openly stated it would allow bond yields to rise and will sell its IndoGB holdings over time. We see this as a significant change in the BI’s stance – the central bank had been buying IndoGBs from the market since 2020. We think bonds can sell off further from here, especially since the market expects further rate hikes at upcoming meetings. During 2017–2019, when BI was not buying bonds from the market, the spread between 10y IndoGBs and USTs ranged between 400–500bp (see Figure 2). Currently, the spread is only 290bp. The bond curve is also flatter now versus 2017-19 period (see Figure 3). Although the current account as a percentage of GDP has improved since then, the fiscal deficit and FX reserves have deteriorated more significantly (see Figure 5). We therefore expect investors to demand a higher premium and think it is better to wait for more attractive levels to buy. The current global environment of rising yields is also unfavorable for the bond market. In the short-term segment, we think the SRBI segment could attract more inflows from foreign investors, as the duration risk is low and foreign investors can purchase them using the discounted FX hedge facility

records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 Are there sources of labor supply that could absorb the extra demand and keep the unemployment rate steady? Domestic demographics are fairly immutable—the aging of the domestic population puts a couple of tenths downward pressure on labor force participation per year. Nor do we see near-term policy change on immigration: border crossings have stalled, and the interior deportations continue. However, the prime-age participation rate (about unaffected by the aging population) been rising in recent months. Over the past year, it has increased by ½ point to 83.9%— slightly more for men +0.7 pct pt than for women +0.4 pct pt. A further half point rise in prime-age participation would allow an extra 45k per month in employment growth. Men’s participation in particular remains low, well below earlier rates. The 89.9% male prime-age participation rate this May compares to 88.3% in 2015 but to 90.7% in May 2005 and 91.8% in May 1995. A one percent rise could allow payrolls to rise at about twice their pace of the past year (or around 100k per month) without pressuring the unemployment rate. records.text: 4 European Watch | 12 June 2026 FX: Familiar territory The SNB once again finds itself in familiar territory: ZIRP versus a strong CHF. With a reluctance to push rates back into negative (we agree), the burden of adjustment falls upon the CHF. It is important to highlight the distinction between domestic and external financial conditions. Whilst domestic policy rates remain accommodative and equity markets buoyant, Swiss domestic financial conditions can be characterised as loose. The external challenge for the SNB is firmly focussed on FX considerations, long the bête noire for Swiss exporters. It is here where the tightening in external financial conditions is top of mind for the SNB. In that context, we continue to see FX rhetoric remaining a key part of the narrative. Whilst the CHF continues to carry the “safe haven” monicker, it is important to contextualise that CHF is essentially a vol of vol currency and historically been more attuned to developments in indices such as the VVIX (see report: Liquid Insight: CHF – Happenstance? 16 April 2026). Despite underlying geopolitical cross currents, underlying market vol pressures remain contained. This has important considerations for CHF. We think the prevailing environment remains conducive to carry trades and with the markets still pricing in a rate hike for the SNB in 2027, we believe CHF underperformance in the near-term is set to continue. We are sceptical that the SNB will validate market pricing.

Bottom line, despite periodic bouts of volatility driven by US trade policy uncertainty, Mexico’s economic performance has remained firmly constructive and has outperformed earlier expectations. A key support has likely been the surge in precious and base metal prices, which appears to have lifted mining export values materially and further underpinned activity over the course of the year. In Brazil, the trade balance surplus has accelerated recently, up 34.2% year-to-date through May, helped by stronger exports. In the first five months of the year, goods exports surpassed imports by USD32.7bn, from USD24.3bn a year earlier. Exports grew 8.7% y/y through May, whereas imports were up just 3.2% in the same period. In the rolling 12 months, the trade surplus stood at USD76.4bn in May, from USD68.1bn at the end of 2025 and USD63.3bn a year earlier.
